title: PermissionSet docs claim there is no public policy or generic grant constructor, yet `from_policy` is exactly that (96 caller files)
description: The type doc says every non-empty constructor is private and that the type has no public policy constructor. The `from_policy` doc says it serves only `InteractionMode::permission_ceiling` 'without exposing a generic grant constructor'. In fact `pub fn from_policy` takes any iterator of permissions and is the de-facto grant constructor across the workspace: 96 files call it, many in production paths that pass the result straight into `SandboxSpec::from_resolved`. The intra-doc link `[harw_core::mode::InteractionMode::permission_ceiling]` also cannot resolve, because harw-authority does not depend on harw-core. Reviewers who rely on this doc will underestimate the grant surface.
evidence: lines 105-111: "all constructors for nonempty grants are private to this crate, except for [`Self::from_policy`] ... This type deliberately implements neither `Deserialize`, `Default`, `FromIterator`, nor a public policy constructor." | lines 129-133: "used by [`harw_core::mode::InteractionMode::permission_ceiling`] ... without exposing a generic grant constructor" / `pub fn from_policy(permissions: impl IntoIterator<Item = Permission>) -> Self` | harw-tool-process/src/provider.rs:548 and harw-job-executor-bwrap/src/executor.rs:201: `SandboxSpec::from_resolved(binding, PermissionSet::from_policy(permissions))`
fix: Rewrite both doc blocks to match reality. `from_policy` is a public, unrestricted constructor for code-defined grants and ceilings. The trust boundary lies with the callers of `SandboxSpec::from_resolved*` and `PolicyBootstrap`, not with this type. Delete the "nor a public policy constructor" clause, and turn the harw_core link into plain code text.
test_idea: Doc-only change; no new test. Central build: `cargo test -p harw-authority --doc`.
reasons: Refuted. The finding claims the PermissionSet docs deny any public constructor while `from_policy` is a hidden generic one, but the doc text (harw-authority/src/lib.rs:105-111 and 126-133) explicitly discloses `from_policy` twice as the public exception ("except for `Self::from_policy`"; "A publicly constructible set of permissions"). The narrower phrases the finding hangs the contradiction on ("public policy constructor" = one built from a deserialized/untrusted RawPolicy blob, kept private behind PolicyBootstrap at lib.rs:1109-1186/1196; "generic grant constructor" = a blanket FromIterator/Default/Deserialize impl, none of which exist) are not violated by `from_policy`, which only takes in-code Permission values. The finding's supporting evidence also fails on inspection: harw-tool-process/src/provider.rs:548 is inside `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` (starts at provider.rs:486-487), not a production path as claimed; harw-job-executor-bwrap/src/executor.rs:201 is production code but builds exactly the documented "code-defined ceiling not derived from a deserialized policy" case, so it confirms rather than contradicts the doc. The 96-caller count is accurate but doesn't make the doc false, since it never claims InteractionMode::permission_ceiling is the sole caller. The one genuinely verifiable defect - the intra-doc link `[harw_core::mode::InteractionMode::permission_ceiling]` at lib.rs:129 cannot resolve because harw-authority/Cargo.toml has no harw-core dependency (dependency runs the other way, harw-core/Cargo.toml:12) - is real but is a minor, differently-scoped cosmetic issue, not the "docs deny an existing public constructor" contradiction the finding is built on, and the repo's CLAUDE.md build gates don't include a rustdoc -D warnings step.

Confirmed, not refuted. Verified independently at /home/user/Harwness/harw-authority/src/lib.rs:105-135:

1. Broken intra-doc link is structural, not a nitpick: harw-authority/Cargo.toml has only [dependencies] harw-types, blake3, ipnet, serde, toml (no harw-core, no dev-dependency on it either). `grep -rn "harw_core" harw-authority/` finds exactly one hit — the doc link at lib.rs:129 `[harw_core::mode::InteractionMode::permission_ceiling]`. Since harw-authority does not depend on harw-core at all, rustdoc has no crate-graph edge to resolve that path; the link is unresolvable by construction, independent of any subjective reading.

2. The "96 callers" claim is essentially accurate: `grep -l 'PermissionSet::from_policy'` across the repo returns 97 files; subtracting the definition site (harw-authority/src/lib.rs itself) and one non-code doc file (docs/design/dod-system-operations-authority.md) leaves ~95 real caller files, matching the finding's "96 caller files" within rounding. Confirmed production call sites: harw-tool-process/src/provider.rs:548 and harw-job-executor-bwrap/src/executor.rs:201 both call `SandboxSpec::from_resolved(binding, PermissionSet::from_policy(permissions))` directly, far from harw-core's `InteractionMode::permission_ceiling` (harw-core/src/mode.rs:345-356), which is only two of many callers.

3. Textual self-contradiction confirmed by reading the block verbatim: line 105-108 explicitly carves out `Self::from_policy` as the one public exception to "all constructors... are private," yet line 110-111 says the type implements "neither `Deserialize`, `Default`, `FromIterator`, nor a public policy constructor" — immediately after naming a public constructor. The `from_policy` doc itself (lines 126-131) says it is "used by [InteractionMode::permission_ceiling]... without exposing a generic grant constructor," but the implementation (line 133-135, `from_validated_policy` at 161-165) takes an unrestricted `impl IntoIterator<Item = Permission>` and applies no validation — it is, mechanically, a generic/unrestricted public grant constructor, and it is used that way by dozens of unrelated crates.

Adversarial checks that could have refuted this did not pan out:
- No decision doc (docs/planning/70-decisions/DEC-001..008) or design doc (runtime-contracts.md, hardening-gap-analysis.md, dod-system-operations-authority.md, agent-composition-contract.md, harw-dod-charter.md, telegram-sandbox-work-requests.md) discusses or justifies this specific doc wording or the broken link; none treat `from_policy`'s broad use as a documented, intentional deviation from the type doc.
- The one plausible steelman — that "policy constructor" means specifically a constructor from a *serialized/deserialized* Policy (matching this crate's own vocabulary: `PolicyBootstrap`/`RawPolicy` at lib.rs:1101-1202, which parses trusted TOML with symlink/ownership checks) as opposed to a raw `Permission` iterator — does not rescue the "without exposing a generic grant constructor" clause or the dead `harw_core` link; both remain factually wrong regardless of that reading.

This is a pure comment/doc-comment fix confined to harw-authority/src/lib.rs (rewrite the type doc at ~105-111 and the from_policy doc at ~126-131); no other file needs to change, matching the finding's own single_file:true claim. Read-only review only; no files were edited, and no cargo/rustc command was run.

Confirmed, not refuted. Read harw-authority/src/lib.rs:105-135 directly (file is unmodified vs HEAD per `git status`/`git diff`, so no concurrent-edit risk).

Doc text (lib.rs:105-111): "Its representation and all constructors for nonempty grants are private to this crate, except for [`Self::from_policy`] ... This type deliberately implements neither `Deserialize`, `Default`, `FromIterator`, nor a public policy constructor." The from_policy docstring itself (lib.rs:126-131) says: "This is used by [`harw_core::mode::InteractionMode::permission_ceiling`] to express mode-specific ceilings without exposing a generic grant constructor."

Two verifiable defects:
1. Link-resolution claim: harw-authority/Cargo.toml deps are only blake3, harw-types, ipnet, serde, toml — no harw-core. An intra-doc link `[harw_core::mode::InteractionMode::permission_ceiling]` from a crate that doesn't depend on harw_core cannot resolve; rustdoc will flag it as unresolved. Verified via `cat harw-authority/Cargo.toml`.
2. "used by ... without exposing a generic grant constructor" is false as a description of actual usage. `pub fn from_policy(permissions: impl IntoIterator<Item = Permission>) -> Self` (lib.rs:133) is exactly a generic, unrestricted grant constructor and is called directly — not via `InteractionMode::permission_ceiling` — from production code outside harw_core. Verified: `grep -rl 'PermissionSet::from_policy\|\.from_policy(' --include='*.rs'` returns exactly 96 files (matches the finding's cited count). Confirmed a genuine non-test production call site: harw-job-executor-bwrap/src/executor.rs:201, `let sandbox = SandboxSpec::from_resolved(binding, PermissionSet::from_policy(permissions));`, sits inside `impl BwrapExecutor` (starts executor.rs:76), well before the `#[cfg(test)] mod tests;` at executor.rs:584 — this is a job-policy-to-sandbox mapping in production code, entirely unrelated to harw_core::mode. (The other cited site, harw-tool-process/src/provider.rs:548, is inside `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` starting at line 486, so that one example is test-only — but the executor.rs case alone already falsifies the "used by permission_ceiling ... without exposing a generic grant constructor" claim, and dozens of the other 96 call sites, e.g. harw-tool-fs/*, harw-tool-shell/*, harw-ops/*, harw-runtime/*, harw-sandbox/bwrap.rs, are likewise unrelated to harw_core::mode.)

This is a genuine M3 (docs contradict code) defect in a security-relevant authority crate: a reviewer trusting the docstring would believe from_policy is scoped to one mode-ceiling call site inside harw_core, when it is in fact the workspace's general-purpose way to mint a code-vouched PermissionSet, feeding SandboxSpec::from_resolved from many independent crates. Not style noise.

Scope check: the fix is confined to rewriting the two doc comments at lib.rs:105-111 and lib.rs:126-131. No function signature, visibility, or behavior changes are implied, so no caller in any of the 96 files needs to change. fixable_in_one_file = true, matching the finding's own "single_file: true; other files: none" claim.

title: WorkspaceBinding derives Deserialize, bypassing the registry canonicalization its doc says is required
description: The doc says that building a binding requires a registry built from trusted operator configuration. `WorkspaceRegistry::build` (around lines 640-660) canonicalizes the root, requires a directory, and requires the root to lie under harness_root. The `#[derive(Deserialize)]` skips all of that: a payload such as `{"tenant":"t","workspace":"w","canonical_root":"/"}` yields a binding whose `ensure_contained` accepts every path. `SandboxSpec::from_resolved` (a pub function) then turns it into a Runtime-origin sandbox. The derive exists only so that `AuthoritySnapshot` can be serialized, and AuthoritySnapshot has no user outside the crate.
evidence: lines 522-526: "Constructing a binding requires a registry built from trusted operator configuration" / `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)] pub struct WorkspaceBinding { tenant, workspace, canonical_root: PathBuf }` | ensure_contained: `if canonical.starts_with(&self.canonical_root)`
fix: Remove `Deserialize` from WorkspaceBinding. Have AuthoritySnapshot persist a plain serializable `(TenantId, WorkspaceId)` reference instead, and have `reissue` compare that reference with the tenant and workspace of the freshly resolved binding. Add a compile_fail doctest next to the existing ones.
test_idea: A compile_fail doctest `needs_deserialize::<WorkspaceBinding>()`. A reissue round-trip test in which the snapshot's workspace reference does not match (TestResult). Central build: `cargo test -p harw-authority` (including doctests).
reasons:
Finding confirmed on the current working tree (harw-authority/src/lib.rs is unmodified by the round-R15 uncommitted diff, so this is the committed state — `git status`/`git diff` show no pending changes to this file).

Evidence checked line-by-line:
- lib.rs:522-530: doc comment "Constructing a binding requires a registry built from trusted operator configuration; wire payloads cannot create a grant merely by deserializing this scope value." immediately above `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)] pub struct WorkspaceBinding { tenant: TenantId, workspace: WorkspaceId, canonical_root: PathBuf }`. The finding quotes only the first clause but the second clause ("wire payloads cannot create a grant...") does not hold up under inspection — see below.
- lib.rs:595-604 `ensure_contained`: `if canonical.starts_with(&self.canonical_root) { Ok(canonical) } else { Err(PathEscapesWorkspace) }` — exact match to the finding's quote.
- lib.rs:623-678 `WorkspaceRegistry::build`: canonicalizes `harness_root` (627-632), canonicalizes each candidate root (644-649), requires `is_dir()` (650-654), requires `canonical_root.starts_with(&harness_root)` (655-659). This is the invariant the doc claims is mandatory.
- lib.rs:920-935 `SandboxSpec::from_resolved` (pub): takes any caller-supplied `WorkspaceBinding` + `PermissionSet` and builds `AuthorityContext { workspace, permissions, network_scope: empty, origin: Runtime }` directly — no registry, no policy check. `PermissionSet::from_policy` (harw-authority/src/lib.rs:133) is likewise unrestricted-public, so the only missing ingredient for an attacker-shaped "grant" is an attacker-shaped `WorkspaceBinding`.
- `TenantId`/`WorkspaceId` (harw-types/src/ids.rs, `newtype_id!` macro, `Deserialize` impl at ids.rs:91-98) validate only "non-empty after trim" (`validate_id`, ids.rs:13-23) — `"t"`/`"w"` pass trivially. `PathBuf`'s `Deserialize` performs no path validation. So `{"tenant":"t","workspace":"w","canonical_root":"/"}` does deserialize into a `WorkspaceBinding` whose `ensure_contained` accepts every path, exactly as claimed.
- Cross-crate reachability of the derive is real: `#[derive(Deserialize)]` puts the generated impl in the same crate as the struct, so private-field access is irrelevant — any downstream crate can call `serde_json::from_str::<WorkspaceBinding>(untrusted)` and then `SandboxSpec::from_resolved(that, perms)`.
- The doc's rebuttal ("wire payloads cannot create a grant merely by deserializing") is not actually enforced: it is true only in the narrow sense that deserializing alone stops one step short of a `AuthorityContext`/grant — but `SandboxSpec::from_resolved` is exactly that one trivial, fully public step, so the assurance is misleading, not a real barrier.
- `AuthoritySnapshot` (887-891) is the only actual user of `WorkspaceBinding`'s `Deserialize`; `grep -rn "AuthoritySnapshot"` across the whole repo shows zero call sites outside harw-authority/src/lib.rs (only in that file and in docs), and `PolicyBootstrap`/`reissue`/`.snapshot()` on `AuthorityContext` also have no external callers — confirming the finding's own statement "AuthoritySnapshot has no user outside the crate."
- `reissue` (1150-1165) is not itself vulnerable: it compares the caller-supplied, freshly-resolved `workspace` against `snapshot.workspace` and uses the caller's `workspace`, not the snapshot's, as the actual grant field — so a forged snapshot can't inject a bad root through `reissue`. But that is a different, narrower code path than the one the finding targets (`SandboxSpec::from_resolved`), and does not close the gap.
- Existing compile_fail doctests (1491-1519) already lock down the analogous invariant for `PermissionSet` ("cannot be deserialized either", 1503-1508) and demonstrate the crate's established pattern for proving these invariants — but no such test exists for `WorkspaceBinding`, and one would legitimately fail to compile-fail today (a `WorkspaceBinding` really can be built from JSON and fed into `from_resolved`), confirming this is a genuine, currently-unguarded gap rather than a false alarm.

Net: the finding accurately reproduces on the current tree; it is a real type-invariant gap (matches pattern M1, "success path skips the check" / fail-open by omission — the crate protects `PermissionSet` from exactly this class of bypass but not `WorkspaceBinding`), even though no current call site in this repo actually deserializes a `WorkspaceBinding` from untrusted input (I verified via repo-wide grep: no `from_str::<WorkspaceBinding>`/serde calls anywhere), so the risk today is API-shape, not a live exploit chain through harw-web/harw-oauth/etc.

Fixable in one file: yes. Everything cited — the derive, `WorkspaceBinding`, `AuthoritySnapshot`, `PolicyBootstrap::reissue`, and where a new compile_fail doctest would go — lives in harw-authority/src/lib.rs (layer "I" per xtask/arch-policy.toml:106-107). The proposed fix (drop `Deserialize` from `WorkspaceBinding`; change `AuthoritySnapshot.workspace` to a plain `(TenantId, WorkspaceId)`-shaped field; have `reissue` compare that against the freshly resolved binding's tenant/workspace; add a `compile_fail` doctest next to the ones at 1491-1519) touches only this file and does not require changes to harw-web/harw-oauth/harw-egress/harw-netsec/harw-node-transport/harw-protocol, since none of those consume `AuthoritySnapshot` or deserialize `WorkspaceBinding` directly (confirmed by grep). No test run performed (read-only per task rules); central build should run the full workspace suite plus doc tests (`cargo test -p harw-authority --doc` in particular, to execute the new compile_fail doctest) and `cargo run -q -p xtask -- gates`.

Refuted by intent/documentation + absence of an actual exploitable call path.

Evidence for "documented intent":
- harw-authority/src/lib.rs:522-524, the doc comment directly on `WorkspaceBinding` already states: "Constructing a binding requires a registry built from trusted operator configuration; wire payloads cannot create a grant merely by deserializing this scope value" — the risk is named, not accidental.
- harw-authority/src/lib.rs:921-924, `SandboxSpec::from_resolved`'s doc: "Creates a sandbox specification from a trusted runtime profile. Runtime profiles are compiled into the binary; dynamic callers must instead obtain an `AuthorityContext` from `PolicyBootstrap`." This textually restricts `from_resolved` to trusted/compiled-in bindings, not to values decoded from untrusted wire payloads — exactly the composition ("deserialize then from_resolved") the finding worries about.
- docs/design/dod-system-operations-authority.md:355-365 lays out the deliberate type hierarchy: only `PermissionSet`/`AuthorityContext` are grants; `PermissionRequest`-shaped types "convey no execution right by itself," and `AuthoritySnapshot` is explicitly "not a grant — resumption requires re-evaluating policy." `WorkspaceBinding` fits the same "reference, not a grant" category by design.

Evidence for "handled elsewhere" (the one real persistence path that exists):
- `PolicyBootstrap::reissue` (harw-authority/src/lib.rs:1150-1164) takes a *separately supplied* `workspace: WorkspaceBinding` argument and rejects with `SnapshotWorkspaceMismatch` if it differs from `snapshot.workspace` (line 1155-1157) before ever consulting the snapshot's own embedded binding. A forged snapshot (`canonical_root: "/"`) cannot pass this check unless the caller's independently, trust-obtained binding also has `canonical_root: "/"` — impossible, because `WorkspaceRegistry::build` (lines 623-678) canonicalizes the path, requires a directory, and requires `canonical_root.starts_with(&harness_root)` (line 655-659). So the forged-snapshot path the finding describes is already neutralized for the only field that actually round-trips through serde in this crate.
- Repo-wide search: `AuthoritySnapshot` has zero users outside `harw-authority/src/lib.rs` (confirmed by grep over the whole tree) — the finding's own premise that "AuthoritySnapshot has no user outside the crate" is correct, which means today it is not even reachable as an attack surface.
- Every one of the ~100 call sites of `SandboxSpec::from_resolved`/`from_resolved_with_network` in the repo sources its `binding` argument from `WorkspaceRegistry::build(...).resolve(...)` or a clone of an already-resolved binding (sampled harw-web/tests/identity_routes.rs:164-190, harw-core/src/admission.rs, harw-job-executor-bwrap/src/executor.rs, harw-runtime/src/sandbox.rs, harw-tool-fs/*, harw-ops/*). No caller anywhere deserializes a `WorkspaceBinding` or a bare wire payload into one; `grep -rn "serde_json::from_.*WorkspaceBinding\|toml::from_str.*WorkspaceBinding"` across the tree returns nothing.
- In the crate's own established pattern, types the authors truly want compile-time-proven non-deserializable (e.g. `PermissionSet`) get a `compile_fail` doctest proving `DeserializeOwned` is *not* implemented (lines 1503-1508). `WorkspaceBinding` does not get this treatment, which is consistent with the authors treating it, like `PermissionRequest`, as a non-authoritative reference value rather than a grant — not an oversight of the same class as a `PermissionSet` leak.

Nuance (why this isn't a clean dismissal): the doc-comment's safety claim is enforced only by convention/API-shape (`from_resolved` not being fed untrusted data) rather than by a compile-time guarantee the way `PermissionSet`'s non-`Deserialize`-ness is. A future caller that deserializes a `WorkspaceBinding` from config/network input and passes it to the public `from_resolved` would indeed get an unvalidated sandbox root, since `from_resolved` performs no containment re-check on its argument. That is a legitimate hardening suggestion (e.g., add a `compile_fail` doctest analogous to the `PermissionSet` one, or gate `from_resolved` to crate-private/registry-sourced bindings) but it is a defense-in-depth improvement against a currently nonexistent call path, not a live invariant bypass — hence real=false under the stated intent lens.

If it were to be treated as real, the fix is entirely localized to harw-authority/src/lib.rs (the struct, its derive, `AuthoritySnapshot`, and `reissue`), so fixable_in_one_file=true.

No files were edited; this is a read-only verification. Files inspected: harw-authority/src/lib.rs (WorkspaceBinding ~522-605, WorkspaceRegistry ~607-693, AuthorityContext/AuthoritySnapshot ~788-908, SandboxSpec::from_resolved ~916-1020, PolicyBootstrap::issue/reissue ~1098-1192, compile_fail doctests ~1491-1519), docs/design/dod-system-operations-authority.md:340-379, harw-web/tests/identity_routes.rs:161-191.

Confirmed, not refuted. harw-authority/src/lib.rs:522-530 documents "Constructing a binding requires a registry built from trusted operator configuration; wire payloads cannot create a grant merely by deserializing this scope value," yet the very next line derives `Deserialize` on `WorkspaceBinding` (line 525). Because `#[derive(Deserialize)]` is expanded in the defining module, it gets access to the private fields (`tenant`, `workspace`, `canonical_root`) despite there being no `pub` constructor — so any code that can call `serde_json::from_str::<WorkspaceBinding>(...)` (or via `AuthoritySnapshot`, lib.rs:886-891, which embeds a `WorkspaceBinding` and also derives Deserialize) can forge a binding with `canonical_root: "/"`. `ensure_contained` (lib.rs:595-604) then does `canonical.starts_with(&self.canonical_root)`, which is true for every path when the root is `/`, and `SandboxSpec::from_resolved` (lib.rs:926, `pub fn`) accepts any `WorkspaceBinding` with no re-validation against `WorkspaceRegistry`. This is a genuine invariant-bypass: the crate goes out of its way to withhold `Deserialize` from sibling security types — `PermissionSet` has no public `Deserialize` (backed by a `compile_fail` doctest at lib.rs:1503-1508) and `AuthorityContext` is documented as "neither deserializable nor directly constructible outside this crate" (lib.rs:788-789) — but `WorkspaceBinding` was left without the same guard, contradicting both its own doc comment and docs/design/dod-system-operations-authority.md:364-365 ("AuthoritySnapshot: ... explicitly not a grant"). I could not find any current call site that actually deserializes a `WorkspaceBinding` or `AuthoritySnapshot` from an untrusted/wire source anywhere in the workspace (grepped for `WorkspaceBinding`/`AuthoritySnapshot` repo-wide; `AuthoritySnapshot`/`PolicyBootstrap::reissue` have zero consumers outside harw-authority's own tests), so the blast radius today is a dormant capability rather than an actively triggered bug — but that does not make it style noise: it is a real, exploitable-by-construction hole in a security-critical type whose whole contract is "no wire payload can become a grant," directly contradicting its own doc.

fixable_in_one_file = true: both `WorkspaceBinding` (lib.rs:526-530) and `AuthoritySnapshot` (lib.rs:887-891) are defined in harw-authority/src/lib.rs, and every reader of `AuthoritySnapshot`'s private fields (`PolicyBootstrap::reissue` at lib.rs:1150-1165, `AuthorityContext::snapshot()` at lib.rs:864-872) also lives there. `TenantId`/`WorkspaceId` (harw-types/src/ids.rs:159,163,182 via a shared macro at line 28) already derive `Serialize, Deserialize`, so swapping AuthoritySnapshot's `workspace: WorkspaceBinding` field for a plain `(TenantId, WorkspaceId)` pair, dropping `Deserialize` from `WorkspaceBinding`, and changing `reissue`'s comparison from full `WorkspaceBinding` equality to a tenant/workspace-id comparison against the freshly resolved binding is mechanically confined to this one file. Repo-wide search found no other file that: constructs a `WorkspaceBinding` via deserialization, embeds it in another `#[derive(Deserialize)]` struct, or calls `AuthoritySnapshot::workspace()`/`PolicyBootstrap::reissue` — so no caller elsewhere breaks. (`AuthoritySnapshot::workspace()`'s return type would change from `&WorkspaceBinding` to something else, but it has zero external callers to break.)

title: test-support docs claim PolicyBootstrap is the only production path to a non-empty NetworkScope; ungated from_resolved_with_network exists and PolicyBootstrap has no production caller
description: The docs of `from_resolved_for_test` and of the `test-support` feature (repeated in two dependent Cargo.toml files) justify the feature this way: outside the crate, a non-empty NetworkScope is supposedly reachable only via `PolicyBootstrap::issue/reissue`, and 'the real API allows this nowhere else'. That is false in two ways. (1) `pub fn from_resolved_with_network` (line 946) has no cfg gate, accepts an arbitrary NetworkScope, and harw-runtime/src/sandbox.rs:205 uses it in production. (2) `PolicyBootstrap` has no production caller at all outside harw-authority; the only outside mention is a comment at harw-core-bridge/src/agent_tool.rs:4695. The same goes for the `from_resolved` doc at line 923 ('dynamic callers must instead obtain an AuthorityContext from PolicyBootstrap'): every dynamic caller uses `from_resolved` instead.
evidence: lib.rs:975-977: "und `PolicyBootstrap::issue`/`reissue` bleiben die einzigen produktiven Wege zu einem nicht-leeren Scope" | lib.rs:946: `pub fn from_resolved_with_network(workspace, permissions, network_scope: NetworkScope)` (no cfg) | harw-authority/Cargo.toml:22: "erlaubt das sonst nirgends außerhalb dieser Crate" | harw-tools/Cargo.toml:36, harw-core-bridge/Cargo.toml:40: "erlaubt das sonst nirgends" | lib.rs:923: "dynamic callers must instead obtain an [`AuthorityContext`] from [`PolicyBootstrap`]"

Remove the 'sonst nirgends' claims from the three Cargo.toml comments. Also record in the ledger that PolicyBootstrap, AuthoritySnapshot and reissue have no production caller.
test_idea: Doc and comment change only. Central build: `cargo test -p harw-authority`, then `cargo run -q -p xtask -- gates`.
reasons:

title: Revoked nodes count toward max_nodes forever and nothing can delete them, so max_nodes acts as a lifetime enrolment quota
description: register_node refuses once `state.nodes.len() >= max_nodes`, and that count includes revoked nodes (node_count doc: 'any state, including revoked'). Revocation only sets the state and prunes routes. The node record stays. The state machine requires a revoked node to re-enrol under a new id, so every revoke-and-re-enrol cycle permanently uses one slot. There is no delete endpoint, CLI, or store method; a workspace-wide grep finds no nodes.remove or retain. After max_nodes lifetime registrations (4096 by default), every new enrolment gets 507 capacity_exhausted until someone stops the daemon and edits state.json. The doc on NodeState::Revoked ('Permanently removed from the topology') contradicts the retained record.
evidence: store.rs:103-107 node_count counts revoked; store.rs:320-322 capacity check; store.rs:371-373 revoke only runs `routes.retain`; state_machine.rs:16-17 'must re-enrol under a new id'; state_machine.rs:39 'Permanently removed from the topology'; api.rs:3-18 lists no delete route.
fix: Count only non-revoked nodes against max_nodes and keep revoked ids as bounded tombstones (e.g. a compact id set with its own cap or retention window) so ids still cannot be reused. Alternatively, add an operator-only purge path. Correct the Revoked doc. All in harw-netsec.
test_idea: Open the store with max_nodes=2, register a and b, revoke both, then register c: today this returns CapacityExhausted; after the fix it succeeds, and re-registering a still fails with NodeExists. Central build: cargo test -p harw-netsec.
reasons:
Confirmed on the current working tree, no discrepancy from the report.

- harw-netsec/src/store.rs:103-107 `node_count` doc says "any state, including revoked", and it literally returns `self.nodes.len()` over the whole `nodes: BTreeMap`.
- harw-netsec/src/store.rs:302-328 `register_node`: the capacity check at line 320 is `if state.nodes.len() >= max_nodes { return Err(NetsecError::CapacityExhausted { limit: max_nodes }); }` — this counts every node record regardless of `NodeState`, including `Revoked`. No filter/exclusion of revoked nodes exists anywhere in this function or elsewhere in store.rs.
- harw-netsec/src/store.rs:340-376 `apply_event` (the only place a node's state changes, including revoke): on transition to `Revoked` it only does `state.routes.retain(|_, route| !route.references(id));` (line 372) — routes are pruned, the node record itself is never removed from `state.nodes`. No `nodes.remove`/`nodes.retain` call exists in store.rs or anywhere under harw-netsec (grep confirms zero hits), so a revoked node's `NodeRecord` is retained forever, permanently occupying one slot.
- harw-netsec/src/state_machine.rs:16-17 confirms the design intent explicitly: "`Revoked` is terminal: a revoked node must re-enrol under a new id" — so each revoke-and-re-enrol cycle burns exactly one more permanent slot.
- harw-netsec/src/state_machine.rs:39 doc comment: "Permanently removed from the topology (terminal)" for `NodeState::Revoked` — this contradicts the retained record; the node stays in the topology's `nodes` map forever, just excluded from routing.
- harw-netsec/src/api.rs:1-45 endpoint table and `OPERATIONS` list every route the daemon exposes (health/version/capabilities/list/register/get/activate/drain/complete-drain/undrain/revoke/zones/routes) — there is no delete/purge node endpoint, and `test_wrong_methods_are_405` (api.rs:266-283) confirms `DELETE /v1/nodes` explicitly resolves to `MethodNotAllowed`, not `NotFound`-then-something-else, i.e. deletion was actively considered and rejected as a method, not omitted by oversight elsewhere.
- Confirmed via workspace-wide grep: no `nodes.remove`, `nodes.retain`, `fn purge`, `fn delete_node`, or `fn remove_node` exists anywhere in harw-netsec/src or the rest of the workspace that references this store (only unrelated crates like harw-cli's telegram attachment purge turned up, and harw-security-hub/harw-web only reference harw-netsec descriptively, not as a client with a purge path).
- Confirmed the concrete numbers: harw-netsec/src/config.rs:45 `DEFAULT_MAX_NODES: usize = 4096`; harw-netsec/src/server.rs:210-214 maps `CapacityExhausted` to `StatusCode::INSUFFICIENT_STORAGE` (HTTP 507) with code `"capacity_exhausted"`, matching the finding's "507 capacity_exhausted" claim exactly.
- Verified no concurrent-edit risk for this specific finding: `git status --porcelain harw-netsec` is empty (working tree matches HEAD for this crate), and `git log` shows the last touching commit is an already-committed prior round, so this is not mid-edit by another process.

This is a genuine, reproducible fail-open/no-egress-path capacity bug (pattern M2: limit/accounting split from lifecycle, compounded by a doc/code mismatch on Revoked, pattern M3). It is not a single-file fix as the finding itself states (single_file: false): the accounting fix belongs in harw-netsec/src/store.rs (exclude revoked from the capacity count or add bounded tombstones), the doc contradiction fix belongs in harw-netsec/src/state_machine.rs (NodeState::Revoked doc comment), and if an operator purge path is added it would need a new Endpoint/operation in harw-netsec/src/api.rs plus server.rs wiring — three files in the same crate, so real=true, fixable_in_one_file=false, matching the finding's own claim.

A workspace grep for delete_node/remove_node/purge/gc/cleanup/prune/reap in harw-netsec/src/*.rs finds nothing but the route-pruning above, and a grep for `NetsecStore` usage outside harw-netsec finds none — no other crate (harw-cli, harw-node-transport, harw-security-hub, etc.) or CLI command touches the store, so there is no out-of-crate cleanup path either.

Intent check for adversarial refutation: no decision doc under docs/planning/70-decisions (only DEC-001..008, all about the work driver, none touching netsec) mentions node capacity, quota lifetime, or a purge policy. docs/planning/90-migration-ledger MIG-013 (which landed harw-netsec) describes the state machine, atomic store and network.sock but says nothing about capacity accounting or revoked-node retention as a deliberate tradeoff, and lists no 'Remaining' item covering it. harw-netsec/src/config.rs's own module doc (masterplan §39, drift report D1) and the max_nodes config docs (config.rs:44-45, 80-81) describe it only as 'Maximum number of registered nodes' / 'Default node capacity' with no mention of revoked nodes counting against it or being tombstoned by design. No guide under docs/guides addresses harw-netsec at all. So this is neither documented as intentional nor handled in another layer — the finding stands as a real accounting bug (M2 pattern): max_nodes is nominally a live-node capacity but behaves as a lifetime enrolment quota because there is no code path anywhere in the workspace that ever shrinks state.nodes.

Scope: fix spans harw-netsec/src/store.rs (capacity check and node_count semantics), harw-netsec/src/state_machine.rs (the Revoked doc comment, and/or the re-enrol contract if tombstoning is chosen), and harw-netsec/src/api.rs (if an operator purge endpoint is added) — matching the finding's own 'single_file: false' claim. Suggested home for any new logic: harw-netsec crate itself (its own ring per xtask/arch-policy.toml); no other crate depends on or reaches into its store, so nothing else needs to move.

title: persist() writes state files that load() then refuses (over 32 MiB), and max_nodes has no upper bound, so the daemon cannot restart
description: Two limits in different layers are never reconciled. load() refuses any state.json over MAX_STATE_BYTES (32 MiB) with StoreTooLarge, and the daemon refuses to start (store.rs:26). persist() serializes and renames whatever state it gets, with no size check. The node count is bounded only by config max_nodes, which validate() requires to be at least 1 and nothing more. The worst-case pretty-printed record allowed by the model limits is about 8 KB: 16 addresses x 259 B, display_name and reason up to 4 bytes per char, key_ref with escaped quotes. At the default 4096 nodes that is about 32.7 MB against a 33.55 MB cap. Any max_nodes above roughly 4,150 (or smaller records at larger max_nodes) lets allowlisted peers grow the file past the cap. Every write succeeds, then the next start fails, and the only recovery is editing state.json by hand.
evidence: store.rs:60 `MAX_STATE_BYTES = 32 MiB`; store.rs:455-470 load refuses larger files; store.rs:476-501 persist has no length check before tempfile write/rename; config.rs:184-186 only `max_nodes == 0` is rejected; model.rs:23-31 per-field maxima; store.rs:320 capacity check is node count only.
fix: In persist(), compare `bytes.len()` against MAX_STATE_BYTES before creating the temp file and return an error (e.g. CapacityExhausted or StoreTooLarge), so mutate() keeps the old state. Also cap max_nodes in NetsecConfig::validate at a value derived from MAX_STATE_BYTES and the worst-case record size. Both changes stay in harw-netsec.
test_idea: Make the limit injectable (e.g. an open_with_limits test constructor), register nodes until the serialized state exceeds the limit, and assert that register_node errors, state.json is byte-identical to before, and NetsecStore::open on the directory still succeeds. Central build: cargo test -p harw-netsec.
reasons:
Confirmed on the current working tree (harw-netsec unmodified since 6835b9c; no R15 changes touch it). All cited evidence checks out exactly:

- store.rs:60 `MAX_STATE_BYTES = 32 * 1024 * 1024` (32 MiB).
- store.rs:455-459 and 465-470: `load()` rejects any state.json over MAX_STATE_BYTES with `StoreTooLarge`, checked both via metadata length and actual bytes read.
- store.rs:476-501 `persist()`: serializes to `bytes` via `serde_json::to_vec_pretty`, writes to a tempfile, fsyncs, renames — with **no comparison of `bytes.len()` against `MAX_STATE_BYTES` anywhere** in the function. Verified by reading the full function body.
- store.rs:320-322: the only capacity check in `register_node` is `state.nodes.len() >= max_nodes` — a count check, not a byte-size check.
- config.rs:184-186: `validate()` only rejects `max_nodes == 0`; there is no upper bound derived from `MAX_STATE_BYTES` or record size (confirmed by reading the full `validate()` at config.rs:166-205).
- model.rs: per-field maxima match the finding exactly — `MAX_ADDRESSES = 16` (model.rs:25), `MAX_DISPLAY_NAME_CHARS = 128` (model.rs:23), `MAX_KEY_REF_LEN = 256` (model.rs:27), `MAX_REASON_CHARS = 512` (model.rs:29), host length up to 253 bytes (model.rs:31,96). `check_text` counts `chars()` not bytes and only forbids control characters, so multi-byte UTF-8 (up to 4 bytes/char) is legal, matching the finding's byte-inflation argument. `check_key_ref` (model.rs:216-226) allows any printable-ASCII byte including `"`, so JSON escaping can double those bytes, matching the "escaped quotes" detail.
- Rough worst-case-record arithmetic (~7.5-8 KB, dominated by 16 addresses at up to ~261 bytes each plus a multi-byte display_name/reason) times the default `max_nodes = 4096` (config.rs's `DEFAULT_MAX_NODES`, config.rs:25) lands right at ~32.7 MB against the 33.55 MB cap, consistent with the finding's numbers.
- daemon.rs:29-30 (`NetsecStore::open(...)?`) propagates `StoreTooLarge`/`StoreCorrupt` and aborts `run()`, so an oversized state.json does make the daemon fail to start — there is no fallback or truncation path anywhere in harw-netsec.
- `max_body_bytes` (server.rs) only bounds a single HTTP request body, not cumulative store size, so it does not mitigate the gap.

This is a genuine fail-open/limit-split gap (pattern M2: accounting split across layers — node-count cap in store.rs vs. byte-size cap also in store.rs but in a different function, with no shared enforcement, and no accounting at all in config.rs). Every write via persist() "succeeds" regardless of size; only the next `load()` on restart notices, and there is no repair path other than manual editing of state.json, exactly as described.

The reported primary defect (successful persist followed by unrecoverable restart) is fully fixed by adding one size check in `persist()` in store.rs before the tempfile write — if `bytes.len() as u64 > MAX_STATE_BYTES`, return an error (e.g. `StoreTooLarge` or a new `CapacityExhausted`-like variant) so `mutate()` (store.rs:401-413) keeps the old in-memory/on-disk state via its existing `?`-propagation before `*current = next`. That alone eliminates the "write succeeds, then daemon can't restart" failure mode regardless of `max_nodes`. The proposed defense-in-depth cap on `max_nodes` in config.rs (config.rs:184-186) is a good secondary hardening but is not required to fix the core defect, so I assess this as fixable in one file (harw-netsec/src/store.rs), though the finding's own suggestion of also touching config.rs is reasonable belt-and-suspenders.

REAL. The finding survives adversarial review: no doc, comment, or other layer reconciles the two limits, and the mechanism checks out exactly as described.

Verified mechanism:
- `harw-netsec/src/store.rs:60` `MAX_STATE_BYTES: u64 = 32 * 1024 * 1024`.
- `store.rs:455-459` `load()` refuses via metadata length before reading; `store.rs:465-470` re-checks after a capped read — both return `NetsecError::StoreTooLarge`.
- `store.rs:476-501` `persist()`: serializes to `bytes` (476-481), writes to a tempfile, fsyncs, renames, fsyncs the dir (484-500) — there is no comparison of `bytes.len()` against `MAX_STATE_BYTES` anywhere in this function or its caller `mutate()` (`store.rs:401-413`). `mutate()` only skips committing the in-memory state if `persist()` itself errors (line 408-411); since `persist()` never errors on size, a big write always succeeds and is committed to memory too.
- `store.rs:320-322` `register_node`'s only capacity gate is `state.nodes.len() >= max_nodes`, a pure count, oblivious to serialized size.
- `harw-netsec/src/config.rs:184-186` `validate()`: `if self.max_nodes == 0 { fail(...) }` — genuinely no upper bound, confirmed by reading the whole `validate()` (166-205) and `RawConfig`/`NetsecConfig` (51-86); no other field or derived cap constrains `max_nodes` against `MAX_STATE_BYTES`.
- `harw-netsec/src/model.rs:22-31` gives the per-field maxima the finding's arithmetic relies on (`MAX_DISPLAY_NAME_CHARS=128`, `MAX_ADDRESSES=16`, `MAX_KEY_REF_LEN=256`, `MAX_REASON_CHARS=512`); the ~8 KB worst-case record and ~4,150-node threshold are a plausible ballpark from these constants, and the exact number doesn't matter — the structural gap (no reconciliation, no persist-time check) is what's real regardless of precisely where it bites.
- `harw-netsec/src/daemon.rs:30` `NetsecStore::open(&config.state_dir, config.max_nodes)?` — `run()` propagates `StoreTooLarge` with `?`, so the daemon genuinely refuses to start, matching the module doc's own claim (`store.rs:22-27`) that it "never resets topology silently."
- `harw-netsec/src/cli.rs:35-42` `CliCommand` is only `Run`/`Help`/`Version` — there is no compact/prune/repair subcommand, confirming "the only recovery is editing state.json by hand."

Intent check (why real=false would fail): grepped `docs/planning/70-decisions/DEC-001..008` (build-process and worker-rights decisions, unrelated), `docs/guides` (no `harw-netsec` hits), the crypto masterplan and `docs/architecture/crypto-drift-report.md` (only unit/user/socket naming, no size-limit discussion), and `docs/planning/90-migration-ledger/MIGRATION_LEDGER.md` (only describes the store as "atomic store and network.sock," nothing about the byte/node-count reconciliation). The only other `max_nodes` hits in the repo (`docs/design/config-scopes.md:158,483,849`, `docs/planning/planning-tool-v1.md:201`, `docs/philosophy/coding-philosophy.md:356`) belong to the unrelated `tools.plan.max_nodes` planning-tool config, not `harw-netsec`. The gap-hunt's own M2 pattern writeup (`docs/planning/85-gap-hunt/R15-patterns.md:44-47,192-195`) documents a *different* M2 instance (provider/retry/worker limits under DEC-003, out of this hunt's scope) and says nothing about netsec's store/config split — so this is a fresh, undocumented occurrence of the pattern class, not a re-report of a known/handled one. No other file in scope (`server.rs`, `daemon.rs`, `api.rs`) adds a byte-size gate before or after `persist()`.

Not fixable in place, fixable in one file: the finding's own "Proposed fix" spans two files (`store.rs` + `config.rs`), but a minimal correct fix needs only `store.rs`: add a length check in `persist()` (around line 482, right after `bytes.push(b'\n')`) that returns the *existing* `NetsecError::StoreTooLarge { path, limit: MAX_STATE_BYTES }` (already defined in `error.rs:80-85`, no new variant needed) when `bytes.len() as u64 > MAX_STATE_BYTES`. Capping `max_nodes` in `config.rs` against `MAX_STATE_BYTES` (the finding's second half) is a good defense-in-depth addition but not required to close the hole, since `persist()` alone bounds every write path regardless of `max_nodes`.

Suggestion: fix belongs in `harw-netsec/src/store.rs` (persist-time size gate, reusing `NetsecError::StoreTooLarge`), i.e. the harw-netsec crate ring — no cross-crate or xtask/arch-policy change needed. title: Codex refresh lock is not mutually exclusive: a live holder is treated as stale, and its guard deletes the next owner's lock
description: The lock counts as stale once its mtime is older than 10 s (LOCK_STALE_AFTER). The holder never touches the file, and the refresh POST it makes while holding the lock has no timeout. So any refresh that takes longer than 10 s gets its lock taken over while it is still running. A second process then reads the old refresh_token and sends it again. OpenAI rotates refresh tokens, so this reuse gets invalid_grant and can revoke the whole token family, which logs the user out. Two more races make it worse. (1) RefreshLockGuard::drop calls remove_file unconditionally, so the first holder deletes the lock that now belongs to the process that took it over, and a third process can enter. (2) The takeover itself is check-then-act: is_lock_stale() → remove_file → create_new. Two waiters that both saw the old stale file can each delete the other's fresh lock, so both end up 'holding' it. There are several realistic concurrent callers: parallel job workers, and the proactive plus reactive refresh in harw-provider-http/src/codex.rs:158-181.
evidence: codex_refresh.rs:56 `const LOCK_STALE_AFTER: Duration = Duration::from_secs(10);`; :169-172 `impl Drop for RefreshLockGuard { fn drop(&mut self) { let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&self.path); } }`; :192-195 `if is_lock_stale(&lock_path) { let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&lock_path); continue; }`; :348-353 `client.post(refresh_url())...send().await?` with no timeout while `_lock` (:331) is held.
fix: (a) Put a tokio::time::timeout around the POST and body read that is clearly shorter than LOCK_STALE_AFTER (for example 8 s), so a live holder can never look stale. (b) Write a unique nonce (pid + random + time) into the lock file when it is created. Store the nonce in the guard, and in Drop remove the file only if its content still matches. (c) Take over a stale lock by renaming it to a unique tombstone name (an atomic rename that only one waiter can win) and then retrying create_new, instead of remove_file. (d) After acquiring the lock, re-read auth.json and skip the network call if the access token is no longer inside the refresh window (another process has just refreshed). Alternative: an OS advisory lock (fs4 try_lock, as in harw-netsec/src/store.rs:229) that the kernel releases on crash, which removes the need for any staleness heuristic. That needs a new dependency and an entry in dependency-review.md.
test_idea: Test that a guard whose lock file was replaced by another owner (different nonce) leaves that file in place on drop. Test that two tasks calling acquire_refresh_lock on a file backdated by more than 10 s (set via filetime or by writing and waiting) never both hold the lock at once. Run the tests with a mock HTTP server that sleeps longer than the timeout and check that the refresh fails with a timeout before LOCK_STALE_AFTER.
reasons:
Verified against the current working tree (harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs is unmodified vs HEAD; git diff --porcelain shows no changes to this file, so nothing is mid-edit).

Confirmed line-by-line:
- codex_refresh.rs:56 `const LOCK_STALE_AFTER: Duration = Duration::from_secs(10);` — staleness is a pure mtime heuristic; the holder never touches the file again after create.
- codex_refresh.rs:169-172 `impl Drop for RefreshLockGuard { fn drop(&mut self) { let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&self.path); } }` — unconditional removal by path, no nonce/content check, so it can delete a lock file that a takeover process created after the original was deemed stale.
- codex_refresh.rs:192-196 (finding cites 192-195, off by exactly one line — text is verbatim correct, just the quoted snippet starts one line early): the `AlreadyExists` arm does `is_lock_stale(&lock_path)` → `remove_file` → `continue` → loop retries `create_new`. This is check-then-act; `create_new`'s atomicity means only one of two simultaneous takeovers wins the *new* file, but the still-running original holder's eventual `Drop` then deletes that winner's file unconditionally (same path), letting a third waiter in while the second is still "holding" in memory — exactly the cascade the finding describes, even though the literal phrase "both end up holding it" simplifies the mechanics slightly.
- codex_refresh.rs:331 `let _lock = acquire_refresh_lock(...).await?;` then :348-353 `client.post(refresh_url())...send().await?` — verified exact text match, no `.timeout()` call anywhere on this request or on the `reqwest::Client`.

The only place timeouts are applied is per-request via `send_with_timeout` (lib.rs:4332-4342), which the refresh path never goes through — `refresh_codex_tokens` calls `client.post(...).send()` directly.
- Confirmed realistic concurrent callers: harw-provider-http/src/codex.rs:158-167 (`headers` → proactive refresh via `access_token_needs_refresh`) and :177-182 (`refresh`, called reactively on 401 from lib.rs:4219-4227). `CodexRoute` (codex.rs:76) holds no in-process mutex, so the file lock in harw-oauth is the sole mutual-exclusion mechanism across both call sites and across processes, matching the module's own doc comment (codex_refresh.rs:23-28) that this lock exists specifically to protect "mehrere Prozesse/Threads."
- Confirmed the fs4-based alternative is a real existing pattern: harw-netsec/src/store.rs:220-234 uses `FileExt::try_lock` from the `fs4` crate (already a workspace dependency, Cargo.toml:190, and harw-netsec/Cargo.toml:34), so the "Alternative" fix in the finding is technically sound (though adding it to harw-oauth would still need a Cargo.toml edit + dependency-review.md entry for that new per-crate dependency, as the finding itself notes).

No test in the file (`test_acquire_refresh_lock_round_trips` etc.) exercises concurrent/stale-lock takeover, so nothing currently guards against this.

Net: every cited line and quoted snippet checks out against the live tree (one citation is off by a single line, `192-195` vs actual `193-196`, but the quoted code text itself is verbatim correct), and the described concurrency defect is real and reproducible by inspection: no timeout bounds the POST, staleness is a blind mtime check, and Drop deletes by path with no ownership token. real=true.

Fixable in one file: yes. title: Context table has only a global cap: one policy peer can fill it and cause TableFull for all other peers
description: ContextTable enforces a single process-wide max_entries (default 10,000). There is no per-owner quota and no rate limit anywhere on POST /v1/contexts. Any uid with a policy rule can issue contexts in a loop with ttl_secs up to max_ttl_secs (default 900 s). Once the table is full, every other peer gets 503 table_full for up to 15 minutes. That includes the harw-web identity path: with require_context=true all web access is then denied (identity.rs HubFailure/ContextRequired). Revoked tombstones also keep counting until they expire.
evidence: table.rs:111-115 `if self.entries.len() >= self.max_entries { self.purge_expired(now); if self.entries.len() >= self.max_entries { return Err(TableFull); } }`; server.rs:531 `if state.table().insert(context, peer.uid, now) == Err(TableFull)`; policy.rs:56 `DEFAULT_MAX_TTL_SECS: u64 = 900`; table.rs:30 `DEFAULT_MAX_CONTEXTS: usize = 10_000`.
fix: Track live entries per owner_uid in ContextTable (for example HashMap<u32, usize>, decremented on purge) and refuse inserts over a per-owner cap (new `max_contexts_per_peer` in config, default for example 64 or max_contexts / 16) with a distinct error such as `peer_quota_exceeded`. Wire the cap through config.rs and server.rs.
test_idea: Create a table with a per-peer cap of 2: owner 1 inserts 2 contexts, the third insert by owner 1 fails with the quota error, and an insert by owner 2 still succeeds. After purge at expiry, owner 1 can insert again.
reasons:
Confirmed on the current working tree (harw-security-hub/table.rs, config.rs, policy.rs, server.rs are all unmodified per `git status`, so this is the shipping state, not a round-R15 work-in-progress).

Evidence matches verbatim:
- table.rs:111-115: `if self.entries.len() >= self.max_entries { self.purge_expired(now); if self.entries.len() >= self.max_entries { return Err(TableFull); } }` — the only guard on insert; keyed purely on total live entry count, no owner_uid dimension anywhere in `ContextTable` (struct at table.rs:79-82 has just `entries: HashMap<SecurityContextId, Entry>` and `max_entries: usize`).
- table.rs:30: `pub const DEFAULT_MAX_CONTEXTS: usize = 10_000;` — single global default, confirmed wired through config.rs:60-62/116-117 (`server.max_contexts`) with no analogous per-peer field anywhere in `ServerConfig` (config.rs:99-118) or `SecurityPolicy`/`PeerRule` (policy.rs:98-141, which has per-peer `tenant`, `workspace`, `trust_zone`, `max_ttl_secs` but nothing quota-like).
- server.rs:531-534: `if state.table().insert(context, peer.uid, now) == Err(TableFull) { ... return error_response(StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, "table_full"); }` — exact match; `issue_context` (server.rs:498-546) performs `PolicyEngine::evaluate_at` (which only checks the per-uid rule's own TTL/workspace/zone, policy.rs:397-456) then inserts into the shared table with no per-owner counting anywhere in between.
- policy.rs:56: `pub const DEFAULT_MAX_TTL_SECS: u64 = 900;` — confirmed; a peer can hold entries up to 900s each, so a sustained ~11 req/s from one uid can keep 10,000 slots occupied indefinitely.
- Revoked entries: `revoke()` (table.rs:146-156) only flips `entry.revoked = true`; `purge_expired()` (table.rs:160-165) removes by `is_expired`, not by `revoked`, so tombstones keep occupying a slot until their original expiry — matches the "revoked tombstones also keep counting" claim, and is exercised by the existing test `test_revocation_is_sticky_until_purge` (table.rs:243-263), which proves this is intended/known behavior, not a fluke.
- Searched the whole crate for any mitigation (`rate_limit|quota|per_peer|per_owner|throttle|Semaphore|governor`, case-insensitive) — zero hits outside the `owner_uid` field used only for ownership checks (may_access, server.rs:548-550), not counting/limiting. No per-uid concurrency cap on the listener either. No design doc in docs/planning/70-decisions or the migration ledger addresses or accepts this risk (grep for table_full/max_contexts/per-peer quota across docs/ turned up only two unrelated design docs).

One overstatement worth flagging: the finding says the harw-web identity path is affected "with require_context=true", citing HubFailure/ContextRequired (harw-web/src/identity.rs:508-554). That path calls `ContextVerifier::verify` → `GET /v1/contexts/{id}` (server.rs:552-567), which only does `table.lookup` (table.rs:130-137) — it never inserts, so it is NOT blocked by TableFull directly; `ContextRequired`/`HubFailure` there are for a missing header or a verify-call error, not for insert saturation. The realistic mechanism is indirect: whatever mints the context a web caller later presents (a POST to `/v1/contexts`, e.g. from harw-oauth/harw-authority, out of my read scope to fully trace) would get 503 `table_full`, so no fresh context would ever reach harw-web to present — not that already-issued, still-valid contexts stop verifying. This nuance doesn't change the core M2 bug (global-only cap, no per-owner accounting, no rate limit on POST /v1/contexts), which is real and reproduces exactly as cited.

Fixable in one file: no. As the finding itself states, a real fix needs table.rs (per-owner counting structure and a distinct error variant), config.rs (new `max_contexts_per_peer` field with validation), and server.rs (wiring the new cap/error into `issue_context`'s response mapping) — three files, matching the finding's own `single_file: false` / "other files" list.

Files read: /home/user/Harwness/harw-security-hub/src/table.rs, /home/user/Harwness/harw-security-hub/src/config.rs, /home/user/Harwness/harw-security-hub/src/policy.rs, /home/user/Harwness/harw-security-hub/src/server.rs, /home/user/Harwness/harw-web/src/identity.rs.

REFUTATION ATTEMPT FAILED — finding stands as real.

Verified mechanics: `ContextTable::insert` (harw-security-hub/src/table.rs:105-126) checks only the process-wide count: `if self.entries.len() >= self.max_entries { self.purge_expired(now); if self.entries.len() >= self.max_entries { return Err(TableFull); } }` (table.rs:111-115). `Entry` does store `owner_uid` (table.rs:35, set at table.rs:121), but the only consumer is `owner_of()` (table.rs:141-143), used elsewhere for verify/revoke authorization, not for accounting live entries per uid. There is no per-owner counter, no eviction-by-owner, no rate limit. `default_max_entries` is `DEFAULT_MAX_CONTEXTS = 10_000` (table.rs:30), overridable only as one process-wide `server.max_contexts` in config.rs:116-117/204-206 — again global, no per-peer field exists in `ServerConfig` or `PeerRule` (checked policy.rs:118-141, config.rs:99-118). `server.rs:531` confirms the call site: `if state.table().insert(context, peer.uid, now) == Err(TableFull) { … return error_response(StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, "table_full"); }`, and `policy.rs:56` confirms `DEFAULT_MAX_TTL_SECS: u64 = 900`. All four evidence lines in the finding check out exactly as cited.

Checked for a mitigating layer and found none:
- No connection-level or per-uid concurrency limiter in the accept loop (harw-security-hub/src/server.rs:261-330); `accept()` just spawns a task per connection with no per-peer cap.
- No rate limiting anywhere in the crate (grepped the whole crate and adjacent docs for "rate_limit"/"quota"/"per-peer"; no hits inside harw-security-hub).
- `PolicyEngine::evaluate_at` (policy.rs:397-456) enforces TTL/workspace/zone narrowing but has no notion of "how many contexts this uid already holds."

Checked intent/documentation and found none supporting "deliberate":
- harw-security-hub/README.md documents `max_contexts` only as one global default (line 85) and lists `table_full` (503) as a possible error (line 44) with no caveat that it is a known, accepted per-peer-DoS tradeoff.
- No decision doc in docs/planning/70-decisions (DEC-001..DEC-008) mentions the context table, per-peer quotas, or this availability tradeoff.
- The masterplan (docs/planning/30-crypto-infrastructure/…_v2.md) has no §on SecurityHub context-table sizing/fairness; grepped "security" near trust/abuse/flood/exhaust/availability and found nothing hub-specific.
- docs/architecture/crypto-drift-report.md (D1/D2, cited in table.rs's own doc comment and README) only covers socket placement, not table capacity/fairness.

Considered "peers are trusted, so this doesn't matter" as a possible refutation: policy peers are host-admin-configured, SO_PEERCRED-authenticated local uids (policy.rs PeerRule), not anonymous internet callers — a real mitigating factor for severity, but not for realness: nothing in code or docs asserts this makes per-peer accounting unnecessary, and a single misbehaving/compromised/buggy trusted peer still degrades every other peer's identity path. This matches the R15 pattern file's M2 ("limit/accounting logic split across layers") rather than its P4 ("intent shows this is deliberate defense-in-depth") — no intent evidence surfaced to invoke P4.

Confirmed the downstream availability claim (harw-web) is structurally correct, with one nuance: harw-web's SecurityHubResolver (harw-web/src/identity.rs:520-573) only *verifies* a context id a caller already presents (`self.verifier.verify(context_id)`, identity.rs:543) — it never calls `POST /v1/contexts` itself. So `TableFull` does not instantly break in-flight verifications; it only stops *new* issuance. But every context is short-lived (`default_ttl_secs` 300s, capped at `max_ttl_secs` 900s, policy.rs:54-56), so once a peer's presented context expires it must go get a new one from the hub, and that renewal is exactly the call `TableFull` blocks — with `require_context = true` that peer then hits `IdentityError::ContextRequired`/`HubFailure` via `without_context` (identity.rs:508-518, 532, 552-554). So "every other peer eventually denied for up to ~15 min" is accurate as contexts churn, not literally instantaneous for all peers as the description's phrasing might suggest — a minor precision nit, not a refutation.

Confirmed no round-R15 edits touch this: `git status --porcelain` and `git diff` show zero uncommitted changes to harw-security-hub/src/{table,server,config,policy}.rs, and `git log` shows the last commit touching harw-security-hub is the R12/R13 infra-daemons commit (6835b9c) — no concurrent fix is in flight to make this stale.

Verdict: real=true. Not deliberate, not documented, not handled in another layer.

Scope/placement: single_file=false is correct — a proper fix needs a new per-owner counter and cap in harw-security-hub/src/table.rs (e.g. `HashMap<u32, usize>` alongside `entries`, decremented in `purge_expired`/on revoke-expiry-cleanup), a new `max_contexts_per_peer` field in `ServerConfig` (harw-security-hub/src/config.rs, plus a `validate()` check), and threading that cap into `HubState::from_config`/`issue_context` in harw-security-hub/src/server.rs (new error code distinct from `table_full`, e.g. `peer_quota_exceeded`, mapped to 503 or 429). This is out of the harw-web/harw-oauth/harw-authority/harw-egress/harw-netsec/harw-node-transport/harw-protocol set but squarely inside harw-security-hub, which is listed in this hunt's assigned crate set.

No tests added (read-only verification task, per the binding rule: no cargo/rustc, no edits). title: security_hub mode with require_context=false: omitting the context header drops the hub-assigned tenant, so the caller runs without a tenant and sees all tenants
description: In security_hub mode, the tenant comes from the verified hub context (identity.rs:576-583). If the header is simply left out, without_context() falls back to TierMapResolver::resolve_peer. That fallback takes the tenant only from uid_tenants and otherwise yields None. By the module's own rule (identity.rs:71-76), a caller without a tenant sees everything. So a local user whose hub principal is bound to tenant A can drop x-harw-security-context and get an unscoped context at the table tier. build_resolver_with does not require a uid_tenants entry for uids listed in uid_principals, so config validation does not prevent this. The fallback exists only for availability, but here it widens scope instead of narrowing it.
evidence: identity.rs:531-533 `let Some(context_id) = presented else { return self.without_context(peer, IdentityError::ContextRequired); };`; :513-517 `if self.require_context { Err(denial) } else { self.fallback.resolve_peer(peer) }`; :378 `tenant: self.tenants.get(peer.uid).cloned()`; :803-817 security_hub branch checks only `principals.is_empty()`.
fix: In without_context(): if the peer's uid has a uid_principals binding, deny (return `denial`) unless uid_tenants also pins a tenant for that uid. Alternatively, reject at build_resolver_with any config in security_hub mode with require_context=false where a uid in uid_principals has no uid_tenants entry (new IdentityConfigError variant). Update the module doc (identity.rs:57-62) to match.
test_idea: Build a SecurityHubResolver with require_context=false, principals {ALICE:'alice'} and no tenants. resolve(peer(ALICE), None) must fail, or config build must fail. With uid_tenants {ALICE:'tenant-a'} the fallback must return tenant-a.
reasons: Confirmed on current tree. harw-web/src/identity.rs:531-533 (missing header -> without_context), :513-517 (without_context: require_context=false -> fallback.resolve_peer), :378 (fallback tenant comes only from uid_tenants, never uid_principals), and :803-817 (build_resolver_with's SecurityHub branch only checks principals.is_empty(), no cross-check that uid_principals entries also have a uid_tenants pin) all match verbatim. harw-operations/src/context.rs:415-419 tenant_admits confirms an unscoped caller (tenant=None) is admitted to every tenant's items, matching the module's own doc at identity.rs:71-76. harw-config/src/web_toml.rs and harw-cli/src/web.rs:404-431 show semantic validation is deferred entirely to build_resolver_with, which performs no such cross-check. Existing tests (identity.rs:923-951, 1089-1102) only cover configs where uid_tenants and uid_principals are paired for the same uids, so the gap is untested. Mechanism is real: in security_hub mode with require_context=false, a peer bound to a hub principal (normally tenant-scoped via the verified context) can simply omit x-harw-security-context to fall back to TierMapResolver, and if the operator didn't also add a matching uid_tenants entry (nothing forces this pairing), the caller becomes unscoped and sees all tenants' data -- a fail-open widening rather than safe degradation. Fixable entirely within identity.rs (either tighten without_context or add validation in build_resolver_with plus a doc update at lines 57-62), consistent with the reported single_file: true.

Refutation attempt failed; the finding stands. Mechanics confirmed exactly as claimed in harw-web/src/identity.rs: without_context() (508-518) falls back to self.fallback.resolve_peer(peer) when require_context=false and no header is presented (531-533); resolve_peer (371-383) sets tenant purely from self.tenants.get(peer.uid) (378), i.e. from uid_tenants only. build_resolver_with (776-819) validates uid_tenants/uid_principals independently (tenant_map/principal_map) and only checks principals.is_empty() for security_hub mode (804-806) -- it never checks that a uid present in uid_principals also has a uid_tenants entry, so IdentityConfigError has no variant for that gap (variants listed at 657-681). Since tenant_admits(None, _) = true (harw-operations/src/context.rs:415-420, tested at context.rs:428-431 "unscoped caller sees every item"), an unscoped ResolvedPeer sees all tenants downstream, matching the module's own doc at identity.rs:71-76.

Intent check (why real=false could apply, and why it does not): the module doc (identity.rs:57-62) does document the require_context=false -> TierMapResolver fallback as deliberate, for availability. But it documents only the tier consequence, never the tenant-widening consequence of that same fallback for a uid that has a hub-principal binding but no uid_tenants entry. Searched docs/planning/70-decisions (DEC-001..008: none mention identity/security_hub/tenant), docs/guides (no identity/security-hub guide exists), docs/setup/web.md (no require_context/uid_principals/uid_tenants mentions at all), and MIGRATION_LEDGER.md MIG-013/014 (harw-web multi-user bullet + "Remaining: tenant filtering... only plumbing and tenant_admits exist" at lines ~200-205) -- none discusses or accepts this specific bypass. docs/planning/85-gap-hunt/R15-patterns.md lists exactly this class under M1 ("Erfolgspfad überspringt Prüfung", with a tenant example at line 35: work_driver.enqueue scanning across all tenants), corroborating this as a real, recognized bug pattern in this codebase rather than an accepted design trade-off.

"Handled elsewhere" check: no other layer re-derives or re-checks the tenant for security_hub-mode fallbacks. harw-cli/src/web.rs:421-435 (web_identity_config) is a pure field-for-field TOML mirror whose own doc comment (405-413) explicitly defers all semantic validation to WebIdentityConfig::build_resolver, which (as shown) does not perform this check. All existing tests exercising this fallback path (test_security_hub_missing_header_falls_back_without_require_context at 1090-1102, test_config_built_security_hub_resolver_handles_unreachable_hub at 1306-1330, and the shared hub_resolver() test helper at 943-951) always pair every uid_principals entry with a matching uid_tenants entry, so the exact gap (principal bound, tenant unbound) is untested in either direction -- no test proves the behavior is intended, and none guards against it.

Scope/fixability: entirely within harw-web/src/identity.rs. A single-file fix (deny in build_resolver_with when a uid_principals key lacks a uid_tenants entry in security_hub mode -- a new IdentityConfigError variant -- plus a doc update at identity.rs:57-62), or alternatively hardening without_context() to require a uid_tenants entry when the uid has a uid_principals binding, is realistic without touching other crates. single_file: true is consistent with what was found; no other file needs to change to fix this.

title: is_public_dns_name doc says [a-z0-9-.] but the code also accepts '_'
description: The allowed character set in the doc and in the code disagree. Underscores are not valid in hostnames (RFC 952/1123), so being stricter here would also be the fail-closed choice for the open research web.
evidence: L228-229 `characters outside [a-z0-9-.]`; L262-264 `.all(|b| b.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || b == b'-' || b == b'_')`
fix: Either drop `|| b == b'_'` (stricter, fail-closed) or document `_`. Dropping it is preferred for a public-hostname check.
test_idea: assert!(!is_public_dns_name("_dmarc.example.org")) after tightening.
reasons: Confirmed on the current working tree (harw-authority/src/lib.rs is unmodified per `git status`, so no concurrent edit affects this). Doc comment at lib.rs:229 states the allowed character set is `[a-z0-9-.]`, but the label-validation code at lib.rs:264 is `label.bytes().all(|b| b.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || b == b'-' || b == b'_')`, which additionally accepts `_`. This is a genuine doc/code mismatch. Confirmed no doctest or unit test in the file (lib.rs:234-245 doctest, lib.rs:1526-1556 `public_dns_name_rejects_literals_local_and_single_label_names` test) exercises an underscore-containing hostname, so behavior is unverified by tests either way and the drift is real, not just a stale comment contradicted by a passing test. Severity/category (low, M3 docs-vs-code drift) is appropriately assigned; the security framing in the finding (underscores invalid per RFC 952/1123, so removing them is the fail-closed choice) is a reasonable secondary observation but the core, verifiable claim is the doc/code text mismatch itself, which holds. Fix is confined to harw-authority/src/lib.rs: either drop `|| b == b'_'` from line 264 or update the doc text on line 229 to mention `_`; no other file references or depends on this specific character-set wording, so `fixable_in_one_file=true`.

Confirmed real, not refuted. harw-authority/src/lib.rs:227-229 documents the allowed label characters as [a-z0-9-.], but the implementation at lib.rs:262-264 accepts `_` too: `.all(|b| b.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || b == b'-' || b == b'_')`. Underscore is not valid in DNS hostnames per RFC 952/1123, so the doc reflects the intended, stricter behavior and the code is the outlier — not the reverse.

Checked for an intent/elsewhere excuse and found none:
- No decision doc mentions this: `grep -rn "underscore\|is_public_dns_name" docs/planning/70-decisions docs/guides` returned nothing relevant; no doc anywhere discusses allowing `_` in public DNS names.
- git blame shows lib.rs:260-266 came from a single commit, 41603a0 ("WIP R9…"), and `git show 41603a0 -- harw-authority/src/lib.rs` shows the doc comment and the `b == b'_'` code were both added together in that same commit — this was never a case of code drifting away from a once-matching doc; the two disagreed from the moment they were written, with no comment explaining the choice.
- Not handled by a caller: `harw-egress/src/policy.rs:323` calls `is_public_dns_name(host)` directly as the sole allow/deny gate for the open research web (`self.is_allowlisted(host) || (self.open_public && is_public_dns_name(host))`), with no separate underscore filtering before or after. `harw-tool-web/src/open_web.rs` and the dod netpolicy crates reference `normalize_host`/related helpers but do not re-validate characters.
- No test exercises underscore-containing hostnames either way (`harw-authority/src/lib.rs:1526-1557`, the only test of this function), so there is no hidden intent encoded in tests either.

Severity is correctly low/cosmetic in the sense that no test currently supplies an underscore hostname to exploit it, but it is a genuine fail-open gap in a security-relevant function (gate to the "open research web"), and the finding's own preferred fix (drop `|| b == b'_'`) is correct and single-line. Confirmed single-file: only harw-authority/src/lib.rs is involved; no other file defines or overrides this character set.

title: Trusted policy is checked by path and then opened following symlinks; the OperatorHome source has no owner or parent-directory check
description: read_trusted_policy checks symlink_metadata and canonicalize on the path, then does a plain File::open, which follows a symlink swapped in after the checks. The fstat checks that follow only look at mode, and at uid==0 for System. For PolicySource::OperatorHome, a file owned by another user that is not g/w-writable passes. The parent `~/.harw` is never checked (ancestor validation runs only for System). So a group-writable ~/.harw lets another group member substitute a 0644 policy that grants permissions and network scope. This is latent: PolicyBootstrap::load has no production caller today (grep finds only harw-authority and a comment in harw-core-bridge/src/agent_tool.rs:4695).
evidence: L1205-1213 symlink check on path; L1214-1223 canonicalize check on path; L1224-1227 `#[cfg(unix)] if source == PolicySource::System { validate_system_policy_ancestors(path)?; }`; L1229 `let mut file = fs::File::open(path)`; L1262 `if mode & 0o022 != 0`; L1267 `if source == PolicySource::System && metadata.uid() != 0` has no OperatorHome owner check.
fix: Open with O_NOFOLLOW (rustix::fs::open with OFlags::RDONLY|NOFOLLOW|CLOEXEC; rustix is a workspace dependency) and compare (dev, ino) from fstat with the earlier symlink_metadata. For OperatorHome, require `metadata.uid() == rustix::process::geteuid().as_raw()`, and require that the parent directory (~/.harw) is owned by euid and has mode & 0o022 == 0.
test_idea: Unit-test read_trusted_policy/validate_policy_metadata on a tempdir: a policy in a 0o777 parent dir with OperatorHome must be rejected, and a policy file whose metadata uid differs from euid must be rejected. The uid check can be tested by factoring it into a pure fn taking (uid, euid).
reasons:
Finding holds; every cited line matches the working tree verbatim, and the gap is genuine.

Map (harw-authority/src/lib.rs, fn read_trusted_policy, L1204-1246):
- L1205-1213: `fs::symlink_metadata(path)` (lstat) then reject if `is_symlink()`.
- L1214-1223: `path.canonicalize()`, reject if result != path.
- L1224-1227: `#[cfg(unix)] if source == PolicySource::System { validate_system_policy_ancestors(path)?; }` — ancestor/parent-dir check is System-only, confirmed by reading validate_system_policy_ancestors (L1280-1302): it walks `path.ancestors()` checking uid==0/mode/non-symlink, but the call site guards it to `PolicySource::System` only. There is no equivalent call for OperatorHome anywhere in the file (grep for `validate_system_policy_ancestors` shows exactly one call site).
- L1229: `fs::File::open(path)` — a second, independent filesystem lookup by path, after the lstat+canonicalize checks above and before the fstat checks below: classic TOCTOU window. A symlink swapped in between L1205 and L1229 is followed by this call.
- L1233-1237 -> `validate_policy_metadata` (L1248-1274, read in full): checks `metadata.is_file()`, `mode & 0o022 == 0`, and `if source == PolicySource::System && metadata.uid() != 0`. I read the whole function body — there is no branch checking ownership for `PolicySource::OperatorHome` at all, confirming the finding's claim precisely.
- No `dev`/`ino` comparison between the L1205 `symlink_metadata` and the post-open `file.metadata()` exists anywhere in the function, so the race is not caught by any other mechanism I could find.

Verified "latent" claim: workspace-wide grep for `PolicyBootstrap::load`, `PolicySource::`, `SYSTEM_POLICY_PATH`, `OPERATOR_POLICY_RELATIVE_PATH` (which is how the vulnerable path would be reached in production) turns up matches only inside harw-authority/src/lib.rs itself: the definitions, and three test-only call sites (`from_test_toml` at L1190, tests at L1632/1656/1675, all under `#[cfg(test)]`/from_policy_bytes which bypasses read_trusted_policy entirely). A broader grep across every crate for `use harw_authority` (150+ hits) shows no crate imports `PolicyBootstrap` or `PolicySource`. The one non-test reference is a German comment at harw-core-bridge/src/agent_tool.rs:4695 that merely cites `PolicyBootstrap::issue` (not `load`) as documentation for why a non-empty `NetworkScope` is possible — not a caller. So the "no production caller today" claim is accurate.

Refutation attempts that failed: I checked whether validate_policy_metadata might have an OperatorHome branch elsewhere (no — read the full function, only System is special-cased); checked whether some other guard closes the TOCTOU window (no dev/ino re-check exists); checked whether PolicyBootstrap::load is reachable via any binary/CLI wiring (no callers found workspace-wide). I could not refute the finding; the code exactly matches every cited line and the described gap is real, though currently unreachable in production since nothing calls PolicyBootstrap::load. That mitigates severity (matches the "low" label) but does not make the finding false.

Fix scope: the core fix (compare dev/ino from the initial symlink_metadata against fstat metadata of the opened fd, and add an OperatorHome owner check plus a parent-directory check analogous to validate_system_policy_ancestors) is fully expressible inside harw-authority/src/lib.rs — no new dependency is strictly required (a dev/ino re-check via std's MetadataExt closes the TOCTOU window without O_NOFOLLOW/rustix). The finding's own suggested rustix-based approach would additionally require a harw-authority/Cargo.toml dependency edit (rustix is a workspace dependency at /home/user/Harwness/Cargo.toml:197 but is not currently listed in harw-authority/Cargo.toml), but that alternative is not the only viable fix, so I still mark this fixable in one file (src/lib.rs). Per xtask/arch-policy.toml:106-107, harw-authority is layer "I" (shared infrastructure), so any fix belongs there, not in a caller crate.

Verified against the current tree; refutation attempt fails on both prongs (deliberate/documented, and handled elsewhere).
