- L1205-1208 fs::symlink_metadata(path)
- L1209-1213 rejects if the path itself is a symlink
- L1214-1223 canonicalize(path) must equal path
- L1224-1227 `#[cfg(unix)] if source == PolicySource::System { validate_system_policy_ancestors(path)?; }` — ancestor/parent-dir ownership+mode check is gated to `PolicySource::System` only; there is no equivalent branch for `OperatorHome`.
- L1229 `fs::File::open(path)` — ordinary open, follows symlinks, no O_NOFOLLOW, no re-check of (dev,ino) against the earlier `symlink_metadata` call. This is a genuine gap between the L1205/L1214 checks and the L1229 open: nothing pins the open to the inode that was stat'd.

A full-repo grep for `PolicyBootstrap::load`, `PolicySource::System`, `PolicySource::OperatorHome`, `SYSTEM_POLICY_PATH`, `OPERATOR_POLICY_RELATIVE_PATH`, and `authority.toml` outside harw-authority/src/lib.rs returns nothing — no caller anywhere in the workspace (including harw-web, harw-oauth, harw-authority, harw-egress, harw-netsec, harw-security-hub, harw-node-transport, harw-protocol, which is this task's area, and the rest of the tree). title: build_client enforces address classes only inside the DNS resolver, so IP-literal URLs skip it unless every caller remembers check_url
description: The egress client puts the address-class check in ScopedResolver. hyper-util never calls the resolver for IP-literal hosts, so for those URLs the only check is the caller-side EgressPolicy::check_url, and the crate only documents that as a caller duty. The enforcement point can therefore be skipped. MistralOcrClient::new is a production caller that builds the policy and client and never calls check_url. Its own doc claims that private address classes stay blocked. A provider base_url such as http://10.0.0.5/v1 or http://169.254.169.254/ therefore bypasses the class rule, while the same host behind a DNS name is refused. Impact is limited because base_url comes from trusted provider config, but the API is fail-open by construction.
evidence: client.rs:15-20 `Für URLs mit IP-Literal ruft hyper-util den Resolver nicht auf ... IP-Literale deckt ausschließlich EgressPolicy::check_url ab`; lib.rs:25-29 lists this under Aufrufer-Pflichten; harw-tool-doc/src/mistral.rs:133-135 doc says `private Adressklassen bleiben gesperrt`; mistral.rs:171-173 `let host = base_url_host(..)?; let policy = Arc::new(EgressPolicy::new(vec![host.clone()], false)?); let client = harw_egress::build_client(policy)?;` has no check_url; mistral.rs:352 `let url = format!("{}/{path}", self.base_url);` is sent directly.
fix: Minimal: in MistralOcrClient::new call `policy.check_url(&config.base_url)?` and keep the checked base URL, so an IP literal goes through check_addr. Structural (harw-egress): export an `EgressClient { client, policy }` whose only request constructor is `request(&self, Method, &str) -> Result<RequestBuilder, EgressError>` and always runs check_url. Stop re-exporting a raw reqwest::Client, which also removes a third-party type from the public API. reqwest's connector_layer cannot see the Uri (Unnameable), so the wrapper is the viable design.
test_idea: harw-tool-doc: MistralOcrClient::new with base_url "http://169.254.169.254/v1" must return Err (Egress AddressDenied). Today it returns Ok.

title: The proxy's idle timeout does not free the relay slot: after the proxy closes, the upstream thread blocks until the sandboxed client writes or closes
description: When the proxy stops sending, relay_connection half-closes the client TCP side and then joins the upstream thread. That thread is blocked in io::copy(client_read), which has no read timeout. The proxy half-closes toward the relay when its target sends EOF and keeps reading until idle_timeout, then drops the Unix stream. The relay cannot see that and only notices on its next write. A silent client therefore keeps both relay threads and its ConnectionSlot indefinitely. The idle limit exists only in the proxy layer, and with 128 slots idle keep-alive connections can use up the relay.
evidence: relay.rs:371-393 (join after half_close_tcp); relay.rs:285-289 and 319-322 slot freed only when the thread returns; relay.rs:78 default 128; proxy.rs:915-918 proxy half-closes and keeps reading; proxy.rs:939-941 idle end drops the session.
fix: Pass an idle bound to relay_connection and set a read timeout on client_read (or poll the proxy socket for POLLHUP), so the thread ends once the proxy side is fully gone. This keeps the change inside harw-egress.
test_idea: Fake proxy that sends EOF and then closes; client connects and stays silent; assert the ConnectionSlot count returns to 0 within the bound. Central build: cargo test -p harw-egress.
reasons:
Verified against current working tree (harw-egress is unmodified in R15, confirmed via `git status`/`git diff --stat -- harw-egress/` = empty).

- relay.rs:358-395 `relay_connection`: spawns an "upstream" thread doing `io::copy(&mut client_read, &mut proxy_write)` (371-380: `client_read` is a clone of the accepted TCP `client`, no read timeout ever set on it in production code — confirmed by grepping the whole crate; the only two `set_read_timeout` calls in the file are in tests, relay.rs:810 and 838, on test-harness sockets, not on the client stream `relay_connection` actually copies from).
- Main thread runs the "downstream" copy `io::copy(&mut proxy_read, &mut client_write)` (383-390), then `half_close_tcp(&client_write)` (391) — this only does `shutdown(Write)` on the TCP socket (relay.rs:400-402), it cannot unblock a pending *read* on the same socket.
- relay.rs:393 then joins the upstream thread before `relay_connection` can return.
- The `ConnectionSlot` is owned by the closure that calls `relay_connection` (relay.rs:285-289: `let _slot = slot; … relay_connection(...)`), and `ConnectionSlot::drop` (319-323, fetch_sub) only runs when that closure returns — i.e. only after `relay_connection` returns, i.e. only after the upstream thread's blocked read is satisfied.
- On the proxy side, `pump` (proxy.rs:876-946) treats upstream-EOF and idle-timeout symmetrically for framing the *proxy's* accounting, but on idle timeout (proxy.rs:939-941) it simply returns `Transfer{end: Idle,...}` from `pump`; back in the caller (proxy.rs:774) that drops the local `client: UnixStream` right after, fully closing the proxy's end of the Unix socket. That produces EOF on the relay's `proxy_read` (ends the downstream copy, matches the trace above) but does **not** touch the relay's client-facing TCP socket at all.
- Net effect: if the sandboxed client (e.g. an idle keep-alive HTTP connection from geckodriver/Firefox) neither sends data nor closes, the upstream thread's blocking `read()` on `client_read` never returns — no EOF, no error — until the client eventually writes (which then fails against the now-dead `proxy_write`, ending the copy) or closes. Until then the thread, and the `ConnectionSlot` it holds (default cap 128 at relay.rs:78, `DEFAULT_RELAY_MAX_CONNECTIONS`, used unchanged by the binary `harw-egress/src/bin/harw-netns-relay.rs:67,78`), stay occupied indefinitely. No OS-level mitigation exists either: no `SO_KEEPALIVE`/TTL is set anywhere in the crate.
- The existing test `test_run_relay_forwards_with_half_close` (relay.rs:794-827) only exercises the client-initiated EOF path (client writes then shuts down write), not proxy-initiated idle closure against a silent client, so nothing in the current suite catches or contradicts this.

title: persist() fails after the rename when the directory fsync fails: disk holds the new state, memory keeps the old, and the next mutation overwrites it
description: mutate() publishes the new state to memory only when persist() returns Ok. persist() renames the temp file over state.json and then fsyncs the directory. If only the directory fsync fails, the new file is already visible on disk, but the caller gets an error and the in-memory state stays old. The next successful mutation is computed from that old memory and silently overwrites the change that was reported as failed. Alternatively a restart revives it, for example a 'revoke' that returned 500 is live after the restart. The module contract claims the opposite ('A crash or a failed write therefore leaves the old complete file on disk *and* the old state in memory').

After a successful rename, set `*current = next` first, then return the fsync failure as a distinct NetsecError (for example DurabilityUncertain) that maps to 500 with a clear message. So the next successful `mutate()` clones the stale `*current` and overwrites the file that already held the (reported-failed) change; a restart instead re-`load()`s the new file and revives it. `apply_event` (store.rs:340-376), which backs the revoke endpoint (`POST /v1/nodes/{id}:revoke`, harw-netsec/src/api.rs:16/42), goes through exactly this `mutate()` path, and `NetsecError::Io` is mapped by the generic `other` arm in server.rs:217-224 to `500 internal`, matching the finding's "revoke that returned 500 is live after restart" scenario exactly.

Intent check (the requested refutation lens) fails to refute it: the module doc explicitly asserts the OPPOSITE invariant — store.rs:14-17, "Only after all of that succeeds does the copy replace the in-memory state. A crash or a failed write therefore leaves the old complete file on disk *and* the old state in memory" — and README.md:84-87 repeats the same claim. No file under docs/planning/70-decisions mentions netsec (grep found none), and docs/planning/90-migration-ledger only records that the atomic store exists (MIGRATION_LEDGER.md:190), never this edge case. The one existing regression test, `test_failed_write_leaves_memory_and_disk_unchanged` (store.rs:580-599), only exercises the branch where the *rename itself* fails (state_path replaced by a directory, so `temp.persist` errors before any fsync) — it does not cover, and cannot distinguish, the rename-succeeds/directory-fsync-fails branch the finding targets. The sibling crate `harw-session-store::durability::sync_parent_directory` (harw-session-store/src/durability.rs:1-95), which the netsec doc comment cites as its model, documents *why* the directory fsync matters (crash durability across power loss) but is used for on-disk record transitions, not for gating an in-process memory cache the way netsec's `mutate()` does — so it is not evidence this divergence is an accepted, transplanted design choice; if anything it shows netsec's in-memory-cache-vs-disk coupling is a novel wrinkle the borrowed contract's wording does not actually cover. So this is a real, undocumented bug, not a deliberate/documented design point and not handled elsewhere.

Fixable in one file: the minimal correct fix reorders the same function pair already in store.rs — split persist() so the caller learns the rename succeeded even if the trailing directory `sync_all()` fails, and in mutate() commit `*current = next` once the rename is durable, then propagate the directory-fsync failure as an error (the existing `NetsecError::Io` variant already maps to `500 internal` via server.rs's generic `other` arm, so no new error variant/file is strictly required for a minimal fix). The doc paragraph needing correction (store.rs:14-17) lives in the same file. README.md:84-87 carries a matching claim; fixing it is good hygiene but is prose, not the code fix, and is not required to close the code bug. I did not edit anything (read-only), and ran no cargo/rustc/make build commands. No tests were added by me; the central build should re-run the existing suite (`cargo test -p harw-netsec`) plus, once a real fix lands, a new regression test that forces `temp.persist` to succeed while the subsequent directory `File::open`/`sync_all` fails (e.g. by revoking directory permissions or closing the dir fd/mocking) and asserts memory now reflects the renamed file while the call still returns an error.

category: rule violation: hand-written errors / third-party types in public API
title: harw-node-transport is the only workspace crate using thiserror, and its public TransportError exposes rustls/hyper/http error types
description: The binding rule requires hand-written error types and forbids third-party types in public APIs. This crate derives all six public error enums with `thiserror::Error`; its Cargo.toml:47 is the only `thiserror` declaration in the whole workspace. The public `TransportError` also wraps `rustls::Error`, `hyper::Error` and `http::Error` via `#[from]`. No other crate depends on harw-node-transport, so fixing it now breaks no caller.
evidence: error.rs:11 `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, thiserror::Error)]` (also at lines 35, 46, 58, 111, 141) | error.rs:118-137: `TlsConfig(#[from] rustls::Error)`, `Http(#[from] hyper::Error)`, `Request(#[from] http::Error)` | Cargo.toml:47 `thiserror = "2"`
fix: Write the error types by hand the way harw-oauth/src/error.rs does, with hand-written Display and Error impls, or use the in-house `#[derive(HarwError)]` like harw-web. Store the rustls, hyper and http causes as `String`, and convert them at the call sites with `map_err`. Remove `thiserror` from Cargo.toml.
test_idea: Existing tests cover the Display strings. Add Display tests for the new String-based variants. Central build: `cargo clippy -p harw-node-transport -- -D warnings`, `cargo test -p harw-node-transport`, `cargo deny check`.
reasons:
Every cited fact reproduces on the current tree, and the "only crate" claim survives a broader check than the finding itself ran.

1. thiserror derives: harw-node-transport/src/error.rs:11,35,46,58,111,141 each carry `#[derive(..., thiserror::Error)]`, and I count exactly six public error types (SignerError, VerifyError, PinError, HandshakeError, TransportError, UplinkError) — matches "all six public error enums."
2. Foreign types in public API: error.rs:119 `TlsConfig(#[from] rustls::Error)`, :134 `Http(#[from] hyper::Error)`, :137 `Request(#[from] http::Error)`, all on the `pub enum TransportError` (non_exhaustive, line 113). This is re-exported publicly at harw-node-transport/src/lib.rs:45 (`pub use error::{..., TransportError, ...}`) and returned from clearly public API: client.rs:90 `pub async fn connect(...) -> Result<Self, TransportError>`, server.rs:90 `pub fn new(...) -> Result<Self, TransportError>`, server.rs:115 `pub async fn serve(...) -> Result<(), TransportError>`. So a caller of `NodeTransportClient::connect` or `NodeTransportServer::new`/`serve` is handed `rustls::Error`/`hyper::Error`/`http::Error` values through `TransportError`'s public variants — a real "third-party type in public API" violation, not just an internal implementation detail.
3. Cargo.toml:47 `thiserror = "2"` is a genuine dependency declaration. I widened the check beyond the finding's own claim: `grep -rn "^thiserror" --include=Cargo.toml .` across the whole repo returns only this one line. Seven other Cargo.toml files (harw-observe-otlp, harw-observe-prom, harw-web, harw-observe-file, dod/crates/harw-dod-{bpf,procmon,flow}) merely contain the *word* "thiserror" inside comments explaining they deliberately avoid it (e.g. "kein thiserror"), which I verified line-by-line — none of them actually depend on it. So "the only thiserror declaration in the whole workspace" holds up even under a broader search than the citation implied.
4. "No other crate depends on harw-node-transport": confirmed — `grep -rln "harw-node-transport" --include=Cargo.toml .` and `grep -rln harw_node_transport --include=*.rs` outside the crate itself both come back empty except the root `Cargo.toml:49` workspace-members list. So fixing this crate's error types cannot break any caller today.
5. The rule itself is a documented, project-wide convention, not an invented constraint: docs/design/crates-inventory.md:18-19 states "Forbidden everywhere: `anyhow`, `thiserror` (hand-written error enums via `harw_macros::HarwError`)", and docs/design/hardening-gap-analysis.md:25/373 cite "consistent hand-written error types (no anyhow/thiserror)" across "all 34 crates" as an implemented strength — harw-node-transport (git log shows it landed in R14, commit f763404, not part of this round's uncommitted R15 diff — `git status --porcelain` shows no changes under harw-node-transport/) is the outlier that breaks that invariant. The proposed fix (hand-written types like harw-oauth/src/error.rs, or `#[derive(HarwError)]` like harw-web/src/error.rs:50, using `harw_macros::HarwError`) matches the pattern already used elsewhere in the workspace I verified by reading those two files directly.

Nothing in the finding overstates or misreads the code; if anything my own independent, wider grep for "thiserror" in Cargo.toml files makes the "only declaration" claim more solid than the citation alone showed.

Scope note: harw-node-transport is in-scope per the brief (listed explicitly under "Your area").

fixable_in_one_file = false: the proposed fix itself lists four files to touch (harw-node-transport/src/error.rs, Cargo.toml, tls.rs, client.rs, server.rs) since the `#[from]` conversions are exercised at call sites in tls.rs/client.rs/server.rs (confirmed via grep: TransportError is used at client.rs:19,90,111,127,131,160,179 and server.rs:20,93,115,141,198,216,219,225,244,277,303 and tls.rs:32,49,53,58,76,93,95,101,108), so removing the `#[from]` impls requires updating every `?`-based conversion at those sites too.

CONFIRMED, not refuted. The finding is real: harw-node-transport is a genuine, undocumented deviation from a strict workspace-wide convention, not a deliberate or documented exception, and not handled at another layer.

Evidence for the convention: harw-macros/src/lib.rs:3-5 states the in-house `#[derive(HarwError)]` is "a dependency-free replacement for `thiserror`." Nearly 50 crates' error.rs module docs repeat "kein anyhow/thiserror" almost verbatim (checked harw-oauth/src/error.rs:1-4, harw-web/src/error.rs:1-9, harw-channel/src/error.rs:3-4, harw-knowledge/src/error.rs:6-8, harw-job-core/src/error.rs:3-4, plus ~40 more found via grep). Many of these hand-written enums do wrap foreign errors (std::io::Error, serde_json::Error, jiff::Error, toml::de/ser::Error, serde_norway::Error) via `#[from]` on a `HarwError`-derived enum — so the actual rule is "no `thiserror`/`anyhow`, hand-write it, foreign causes may be wrapped only through the house macro," which harw-node-transport breaks at the crate-derivation level, not just by touching foreign types.

Evidence the rule is real but unenforced (so this is exactly what the hunt should catch, not noise): docs/planning/85-gap-hunt/R15-patterns.md itself lists "P8 — Regeln ohne Werkzeug, Teil 2: öffentliche Fremdtypen (etwa 8 Funde) ... Wie bei P5 ist die Regel dokumentiert, wird aber nicht erzwungen" (line ~150-155) — public foreign types in signatures is a known, documented-but-unenforced category from this very round, and no `xtask` gate or `deny.toml` [bans] entry currently blocks `thiserror` (checked xtask/arch-policy.toml, xtask/src/*.rs, deny.toml — no hits).

Checked for an intentional exception and found none: harw-node-transport/README.md has no mention of "thiserror" or an error-handling rationale (only a TLS-stack rationale); Cargo.toml:1-13 documents the TLS/crypto choice but not the error-derivation choice; xtask/arch-policy.toml:204-205 only assigns the crate to layer A, no error-policy note; docs/planning/70-decisions has no DEC file about error types; docs/planning/90-migration-ledger/MIGRATION_LEDGER.md's MIG-013 entry (lines 197-199) describes the crate's TLS/handshake/uplink content, not its error strategy. No comment inside harw-node-transport/src/error.rs explains or excuses the thiserror choice. `git log`/`git status` show no in-flight edit to this crate in this round (last touch was the R14 commit f763404), so this isn't a false positive from a concurrent partial edit.

Not "handled elsewhere" either: harw-node-transport/src/lib.rs:45 re-exports `TransportError` at the crate root, so it is genuinely public API; `grep -rl harw-node-transport --include=Cargo.toml .` shows only the crate's own Cargo.toml and the root workspace Cargo.toml reference it — no consumer crate exists yet, matching the finder's "fixing it now breaks no [external] caller" claim.

fixable_in_one_file = false, matching the finder's own single_file:false: TransportError's `#[from]` conversions are exercised via `?` outside error.rs — harw-node-transport/src/tls.rs:54 (`load_private_key(key_der)?`) and lines 61/78 (`.with_protocol_versions(...)?`) rely on `From<rustls::Error>`; harw-node-transport/src/client.rs:134 (`hyper::client::conn::http1::handshake(...).await?`) and :161 (`self.sender.ready().await?`) rely on `From<hyper::Error>`; harw-node-transport/src/server.rs has parallel `TransportError`-returning functions with similar `?` chains. Removing `#[from] rustls::Error`/`hyper::Error`/`http::Error` from error.rs without touching these call sites would not compile, so the fix genuinely spans error.rs, tls.rs, client.rs, server.rs, and Cargo.toml, as the finding states.

Suggested home for the fix: stays in harw-node-transport (ring/layer A, xtask/arch-policy.toml:204 `layer = "A"`); no new crate needed. Rewrite the six enums in harw-node-transport/src/error.rs by hand using `#[derive(harw_macros::HarwError)]` (the pattern in harw-web/src/error.rs and harw-oauth/src/error.rs), store the rustls/hyper/http causes as `String` via `.map_err(|e| ...(e.to_string()))?` at the three call sites identified above, and drop `thiserror = "2"` from harw-node-transport/Cargo.toml:47.

title: jwt_needs_refresh computes `exp - now` unchecked on an untrusted i64 claim
description: `exp` comes from an unverified JWT payload, either in ~/.codex/auth.json or in a token server response, as any i64. A value near i64::MIN makes `exp - now` overflow. In debug/test builds (overflow-checks on) that panics in library code on the request path (codex.rs:188-200 calls it before every request). In release builds the result wraps to a large positive number, so the token is treated as not expiring and no proactive refresh happens.
evidence: codex_refresh.rs:115-122 `let Some(exp) = jwt_exp_unix_seconds(token) else { return false; }; let now = ... as i64 ...; exp - now <= window_seconds`
fix: Use `exp.saturating_sub(now) <= window_seconds`. Optionally treat an `exp` outside a plausible range (for example exp <= 0) as needing a refresh.
test_idea: Add jwt_needs_refresh(make_jwt_with_exp(i64::MIN), 300) == true, with no panic in the test profile.
reasons: Verified on the current working tree: harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs:98-100 decodes `exp` from an unverified JWT via serde_json::Value::as_i64() with no range check, and codex_refresh.rs:113-123 computes `exp - now <= window_seconds` unchecked. `now` is always small and non-negative (SystemTime-derived, guarded by unwrap_or(0)), so an exp near i64::MIN causes subtraction underflow. Cargo.toml's [profile.dev] (lines 226-227) sets no overflow-checks override, so cargo's default (on for dev/test) applies, meaning this panics in library code in debug/test builds; in release it wraps to a large positive number, matching the fail-open description. The call site harw-provider-http/src/codex.rs:188-200 confirms this runs before every request, but no fix is needed there. Existing tests (codex_refresh.rs:440-482) only cover plausible epoch values, not adversarial exp, so nothing currently catches this. The fix (saturating_sub) and a new regression test both live entirely in harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs.

Confirmed real. `jwt_needs_refresh` at /home/user/Harwness/harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs:114-123 does `exp - now <= window_seconds` (line 122) with plain i64 subtraction, no `checked_`/`saturating_` variant, no range clamp on `exp`. `exp` comes from `jwt_exp_unix_seconds` (codex_refresh.rs:98-100 -> `decode_jwt_payload` at codex_refresh.rs:86-90), which decodes the JWT payload segment as JSON and pulls `exp` as any `i64` — the module doc itself states this is done "ohne die Signatur zu prüfen" (codex_refresh.rs:12-13, 84-85), i.e. deliberately no signature check, so the numeric value is not authenticated/bounded by design.

Trust chain confirmed by reading the writer side: `refresh_codex_tokens` (codex_refresh.rs:327-402) takes `access_token` straight from the deserialized `RefreshResponse` (line 366-368) and writes it into `auth.json` (line 376, 395) with zero validation of its JWT structure or `exp` magnitude. So a malformed/buggy token-server response's `exp` claim flows unchecked into the credential file and then into the arithmetic at line 122 on the very next call.

Call site confirmed: `harw-provider-http/src/codex.rs:159` calls `access_token_needs_refresh()` (defined 188-201) inside `headers()`, which the doc comment (150-157) confirms runs before every outgoing request; line 200 calls `harw_oauth::jwt_needs_refresh(token, PROACTIVE_REFRESH_WINDOW_SECONDS)` with no bounds check on `token`'s `exp` beforehand.

Checked for mitigation/documentation and found none:
- No `saturating_sub`/`checked_sub` anywhere in harw-oauth/src (grep empty).
- No profile override of `overflow-checks`/`debug-assertions` in /home/user/Harwness/Cargo.toml (only `opt-level`, `lto`, `codegen-units`, `strip`, `panic` are set for `[profile.dev]`/`[profile.release]`/`[profile.release-runner]`), so Rust defaults apply: overflow-checks on in dev/test (panics), off in release (silent wraparound) — exactly what the finding claims.
- No mention of this function, integer overflow, or an accepted-risk decision in docs/planning/70-decisions, docs/guides, or docs/planning/90-migration-ledger (all greps empty).
- docs/planning/85-gap-hunt/R15-patterns.md documents unrelated pattern classes (M1 success-path-skips-check, M2 split limits, M3 doc drift, M4 hotspot file) and does not cover this integer-overflow case.
- Existing tests (codex_refresh.rs:440-482, codex.rs:590-633) only exercise normal near-`now` `exp` values; none construct an adversarial `exp` near `i64::MIN`, so nothing currently catches or documents this as a known/accepted edge case.
- The reactive 401-retry fallback (codex.rs:154-157) only mitigates the release-mode fail-open consequence (a missed proactive refresh, matching the finding's 'low' severity), it does not touch the separate debug/test-build panic risk from the same unchecked subtraction, so it does not make the finding \"handled elsewhere.\"

Conclusion: not deliberate, not documented, not caught by any other layer. The fix (`exp.saturating_sub(now)`) is a one-line change confined to harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs:122, matching the finding's single_file:true claim.

title: Refreshed Codex tokens go into a fixed temp path opened with create+truncate, so 0600 is not enforced and symlinks are followed
description: write_credential_document always uses `auth.json.tmp-refresh`, opened with create(true).truncate(true). OpenOptionsExt::mode(0o600) only applies when the file is newly created. If that path already exists (a leftover, a concurrent writer after the lock steal above, or a planted symlink), the access and refresh tokens are written with the existing file's permissions or through the symlink. rename() then carries those permissions onto auth.json. Concurrent writers also interleave in the same temp file. harw-oauth/src/store.rs:53-77 already does this correctly with a unique name and create_new.
evidence: L235 `let temp_path = path.with_extension("json.tmp-refresh");`; L237 `options.write(true).create(true).truncate(true);`; L241 `options.mode(0o600);`; L245 `let mut file = options.open(&temp_path)?;`; L255 `std::fs::rename(&temp_path, path)?;`
fix: Reuse the store.rs approach: a unique temp name (pid+nanos+counter) opened with `create_new(true)` and `mode(0o600)`. O_EXCL also refuses an existing symlink. Additionally call `file.set_permissions(Permissions::from_mode(0o600))` on the handle before writing. Retry on AlreadyExists and remove the temp file on error, as today.
test_idea: Pre-create `<dir>/auth.json.tmp-refresh` with mode 0o644, run write_credential_document, and assert the metadata of auth.json has mode & 0o777 == 0o600. Pre-create the temp path as a symlink to a sentinel file and assert the sentinel is unchanged.
reasons:

- L235 `let temp_path = path.with_extension("json.tmp-refresh");` — fixed, predictable name (not unique per call/process).
- L237 `options.write(true).create(true).truncate(true);` — `create(true)`, not `create_new(true)`.
- L241 `options.mode(0o600);` (under `#[cfg(unix)]`).
- L245 `let mut file = options.open(&temp_path)?;`
- L255 `std::fs::rename(&temp_path, path)?;`
No `O_NOFOLLOW`/`custom_flags`, no `symlink_metadata`/existence check, and no `create_new` anywhere in the function (full function read, lines 229-267).

The finding's Unix semantics claim is correct: `mode()` on `OpenOptions` only affects the permission bits used by `open(2)` when `O_CREAT` actually creates a new file; if the path already exists, the mode argument is ignored and the file's existing permissions (or, if it's a symlink, the target it resolves to) are used instead — `open()` follows symlinks by default absent `O_NOFOLLOW`. Since this call uses `create(true)` (not `create_new`) with no follow-guard, a pre-existing regular file or a planted symlink at the fixed `temp_path` is opened, truncated and written through, and its (or the symlink target's) permissions/identity survive the subsequent `rename()`, unlike the finding's simplified read this can even leave `auth.json` as a symlink itself since `rename()` moves the link, not its target, when `oldpath` is a symlink — still a genuine mishandling, just a slightly different failure shape than the finding's prose.

The contrast with harw-oauth/src/store.rs is real and confirmed by reading store.rs:36-77: `temporary_token_path` builds a unique name (`pid` + nanosecond timestamp + atomic counter, L38-51), and `create_restricted_temp` (L53-77) uses `create_new(true)` plus `mode(0o600)` in a retry loop — exactly the stronger pattern the finding describes as already used elsewhere in the same crate. `create_restricted_temp` is a private `fn` (not `pub`/`pub(crate)`), so codex_refresh.rs cannot import it directly today, but the proposed fix ("reuse the store.rs approach") only requires mirroring that pattern (unique temp name + `create_new` + `mode`) inline inside codex_refresh.rs — no change to store.rs is required, so the fix stays confined to the one cited file.

The concurrency angle is also structurally supported, not speculative: `refresh_codex_tokens` (codex_refresh.rs:327-395) acquires the file lock at L331, then performs a full HTTP round-trip (L348-356) before calling `write_credential_document` at L395, all while still holding the lock. `acquire_refresh_lock`/`is_lock_stale` (L180-219) treats any lock older than `LOCK_STALE_AFTER` = 10s (L56) as abandoned and lets a second caller steal it (L193-196) and proceed to its own `write_credential_document` call against the same fixed `temp_path`, so two processes racing a slow refresh can genuinely interleave writes to the same file name, as the finding claims.

This path is live, not test-only or dead code: harw-provider-http/src/codex.rs:178 calls `harw_oauth::refresh_codex_tokens(client, Path::new(&self.path))` directly against the real `~/.codex/auth.json`, and harw-oauth/src/lib.rs:44 wires `mod codex_refresh;` into the crate's public surface.

I could not find any mitigating check elsewhere in the file (e.g., an existence/symlink guard before `options.open`) that would neutralize the issue — the full function body was read and none exists. I therefore did not find grounds to refute this finding; the evidence holds as stated (with the minor correction on what `rename()` does to a symlinked temp path, which doesn't weaken the underlying claim). single_file/fix confined to harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs, as claimed.

Confirmed against the current tree (re-read just now, no concurrent-edit drift). harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs:229-267, `write_credential_document`:
- L235 `let temp_path = path.with_extension("json.tmp-refresh");` — fixed, predictable temp name (not per-pid/nanos/counter like store.rs).
- L237 `options.write(true).create(true).truncate(true);` — `create`, not `create_new`; no `O_EXCL`.
- L241 `options.mode(0o600);` — per POSIX/Rust `OpenOptionsExt::mode` semantics, this mode is applied by the kernel only when `open()` actually creates the file; if `temp_path` already exists (stale leftover, planted file, or a symlink), `open()` silently succeeds against the existing inode/target with whatever perms it already has, and no `O_NOFOLLOW` is set, so a symlink at that path is followed.
- L255 `std::fs::rename(&temp_path, path)?;` then propagates whatever ended up at `temp_path` onto `auth.json`.

This is a real gap, not a documented trade-off or something caught elsewhere:
- Same crate, same file-write problem, correct fix already exists: harw-oauth/src/store.rs:38-77 (`temporary_token_path` with pid+nanos+counter, `create_new(true)`, retry loop on `AlreadyExists`) plus an explicit regression test for exactly this class of attack (`test_save_token_rejects_secrets_symlink_outside_home`, store.rs:250-278) and a permission-mode assertion (store.rs:174-182). codex_refresh.rs has no analogous test — the temp-file/permission path is untested here, only the higher-level refresh-error-path tests exist (codex_refresh.rs:499-534). That store.rs already implements and tests the hardened pattern is strong evidence this is an inconsistency/oversight, not a deliberate per-file design choice.
- No decision doc, guide, or comment sanctions the weaker pattern for Codex refresh specifically. `docs/design/provider-auth-gateway.md:48-51` only notes Codex refresh was added later (scope note), nothing about temp-file hardening. `docs/design/secrets-and-audit.md:65-69` states the project threat model excludes "a hostile co-tenant on shared infrastructure," which could arguably wave off the pure symlink-attack half of the finding — but that statement is scoped to `harw-secrets`' DEK/KEK design, and it's undercut by store.rs (same crate, same author intent) already defending against local-symlink/pre-existing-file tricks. It does not touch the second, non-adversarial half of the finding: a leftover temp file (e.g. from an aborted prior refresh where the L263-264 cleanup itself failed, or two processes racing after the 10s stale-lock steal at L192-206) still gets truncated-and-reused rather than freshly created with enforced 0600, and two legitimate concurrent refreshers can both hold open handles to the same fixed `temp_path` and interleave writes/truncations — that's a correctness bug independent of the co-tenant threat-model carve-out.
- Checked callers: `harw-provider-http/src/codex.rs:170-179` (`CodexRoute::refresh`) and `harw-provider-http/src/lib.rs:4203-4228` (401 retry) call `refresh_codex_tokens` directly and do nothing to fix up permissions or dedupe the temp path afterward; no other layer mitigates this.

Fix is self-contained: codex_refresh.rs already imports `OpenOptionsExt`/uses `OpenOptions` locally, so it can adopt the store.rs pattern (unique temp name, `create_new(true)`, `mode(0o600)`, retry-on-`AlreadyExists`, optional post-open `set_permissions`) without touching store.rs or any caller — single-file change, matching the finding's own proposed fix and `single_file: true`.

title: TokenExchange.body is documented as the raw response body but is always a redacted placeholder
description: The field doc invites future code to put raw provider bodies into errors, even though both constructors deliberately redact because they can contain token material.
evidence: error.rs:16-18 `/// Roher Antwort-Body (für Diagnose; kann Fehlermeldung enthalten). body: String,`; flow.rs:104-106 and codex_refresh.rs:152-154 always return a fixed `... response body redacted` string.
fix: Change the doc to state that the field is always a redacted placeholder and that the raw body is never copied, because it may carry tokens.
reasons:
Confirmed on the current working tree, no refutation found.

- harw-oauth/src/error.rs:14-19: `OAuthError::TokenExchange { status: u16, body: String }` where the doc comment on `body` (line 17) reads "Roher Antwort-Body (für Diagnose; kann Fehlermeldung enthalten)." — i.e. "raw response body (for diagnosis; may contain error message)."
- harw-oauth/src/flow.rs:104-106: `fn redacted_token_exchange_body(_body: &str) -> String { "token exchange response body redacted".to_owned() }` — the parameter is prefixed `_body` and is never read; the function unconditionally returns a fixed literal.
- harw-oauth/src/flow.rs:191-194: the only production call site builds `OAuthError::TokenExchange { status: ..., body: redacted_token_exchange_body(&body) }`, so `body` is always the placeholder string, never the provider's actual response text.
- harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs:152-154 and :358-361: identical pattern — `redacted_refresh_body(_body: &str)` ignores its argument and returns `"codex token refresh response body redacted".to_owned()`, used at the sole call site that constructs `TokenExchange`.
- harw-oauth/src/flow.rs:281-296 (`test_token_exchange_body_is_redacted`) even asserts this explicitly: it feeds a secret-bearing body in and asserts the result equals the fixed redacted string, and that this is by design (comment: "kann Tokenmaterial enthalten" style redaction, matching codex_refresh.rs:151 `/// Ersetzt Antwort-Bodies, die Tokenmaterial enthalten könnten, in Fehlern.`).

Grep confirms there are exactly two production constructors of `OAuthError::TokenExchange` (flow.rs:191, codex_refresh.rs:358) plus one test constructor (flow.rs:284), and both production paths route through the always-redacting helper. There is no code path anywhere in harw-oauth that puts the true raw body into this field, so the field doc's claim of "raw" body is stale/inaccurate — a genuine M3 (docs drift from code) issue, correctly classified as low severity since it is a doc-only mismatch with no behavioral bug (the redaction itself is correct and deliberately guards against leaking token material).

The proposed fix (reword the doc comment on `error.rs:17` to say the field is always a redacted placeholder and the raw body is never copied) only requires touching `harw-oauth/src/error.rs`; flow.rs and codex_refresh.rs are corroborating evidence, not required edits. So real=true, fixable_in_one_file=true, matching the finding's own single_file=true claim.

Confirmed, but weak/cosmetic — the underlying redaction behavior is deliberate and well-documented, only the field-level doc string is stale.

Evidence:
- harw-oauth/src/error.rs:14-19: `TokenExchange { status: u16, /// Roher Antwort-Body (für Diagnose; kann Fehlermeldung enthalten). body: String }` — the field doc literally says "raw response body" without mentioning redaction.
- harw-oauth/src/flow.rs:103-106 `redacted_token_exchange_body(_body: &str) -> String { "token exchange response body redacted".to_owned() }` and its call at flow.rs:191-194 — the body parameter is intentionally discarded (`_body`), always returning the same fixed placeholder.
- harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs:151-154 `redacted_refresh_body` — same pattern, used at codex_refresh.rs:358-361.
- Only two production call sites construct `OAuthError::TokenExchange` in the whole repo (confirmed via `rg TokenExchange` across the workspace — only error.rs, flow.rs, codex_refresh.rs match), and both go through a redaction helper.

Intent check (why this leans toward refuted but not fully): the redaction is explicitly deliberate and documented right next to both call sites, not just buried in the field doc:
- flow.rs:156-157 (public `# Errors` doc on `exchange_code`): "[`OAuthError::TokenExchange`]: nicht-erfolgreiche HTTP-Antwort; der Antwort-Body wird aus Sicherheitsgründen nicht in den Fehler übernommen." (the body is deliberately NOT carried into the error, for security reasons.)
- codex_refresh.rs:317-318 (public `# Errors` doc on `refresh_codex_tokens`): identical statement.
- Comments directly above each redaction fn state the reason: "Ersetzt providerseitige Fehlerdetails, die sensible Werte enthalten können" (flow.rs:103) / "Ersetzt Antwort-Bodies, die Tokenmaterial enthalten könnten, in Fehlern" (codex_refresh.rs:151).
- A dedicated regression test, flow.rs:281-299 `test_token_exchange_body_is_redacted`, asserts the placeholder string is produced and that the raw secret body never appears — this is a tested contract, not an oversight.

So the "invites future code to add raw bodies" risk is mitigated: any contributor reading the public API docs of the only two functions that build this variant sees an explicit security rationale, and a named test would need to be touched/renamed to regress silently. That said, the specific claim in the finding is literally true and not fully refuted: the field-level doc comment on `error.rs:17` itself is inconsistent with the field's actual, always-fixed content and does not mention redaction, so someone reading only the `OAuthError` enum's own rustdoc page (without opening `flow.rs`/`codex_refresh.rs`) would still get a misleading impression. This matches the M3 "docs drifting from code" pattern the hunt was looking for, but is genuinely low severity/cosmetic given the strong documentation and test coverage elsewhere in the same crate.

Scope note: all evidence is inside harw-oauth (in scope for this hunt: harw-web, harw-oauth, harw-authority, harw-egress, harw-netsec, harw-security-hub, harw-node-transport, harw-protocol). No edits were made (read-only task). If accepted, the fix is a doc-comment wording change confined to harw-oauth/src/error.rs:17, as proposed — no code/behavior change, no test changes needed, and nothing for the central build to run beyond the normal fmt/clippy/test sequence since no code changes are involved.

title: Env-overridable token endpoints accept any scheme and host, and responses are read unbounded without a deadline
description: HARW_OAUTH_TOKEN_URL and HARW_CODEX_OAUTH_REFRESH_URL only have blank values filtered out. An http:// or arbitrary URL is used as-is, and the request carries the authorization code plus PKCE verifier, or the long-lived Codex refresh_token, possibly in cleartext. Both functions read the body with response.text(), with no size cap and no timeout of their own. The CLI passes reqwest::Client::new(), which has no timeout, so a stalled endpoint hangs the login and the refresh (the refresh does this while holding the refresh lock).
evidence: flow.rs:36-41 env_or; flow.rs:172-186 payload with code_verifier POSTed to the env URL; flow.rs:189 `response.text()`; codex_refresh.rs:80-82 refresh_url; codex_refresh.rs:342-356 refresh_token POST and unbounded text(); harw-cli/src/auth.rs:93 `reqwest::Client::new()`.
fix: Parse the override with url::Url and require https (allow http only for loopback in tests). Wrap send and body read in tokio::time::timeout and read at most a fixed number of bytes (e.g. 64 KiB) via bytes_stream or a Content-Length check before parsing.
test_idea: Unit-test a new endpoint validator (http://evil rejected, https ok, http://127.0.0.1 allowed only in cfg(test)); run a local stub that returns a 1 MiB body and assert MalformedInput or a size error. Central build: cargo test -p harw-oauth.
reasons:
Confirmed on current tree, all citations match exactly:
- harw-oauth/src/flow.rs:36-41 `env_or` only filters blank values, no scheme/host check.
- harw-oauth/src/flow.rs:182 `.post(env_or("HARW_OAUTH_TOKEN_URL", DEFAULT_TOKEN_URL))` posts to the raw env-supplied string; lines 172-179 build the payload with `code`, `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `code_verifier` (PKCE verifier). Line 189 `let body = response.text().await?;` reads the body fully with no size cap, and the function contains no `tokio::time::timeout` or similar deadline anywhere in its body (lines 163-203 read in full).
- harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs:80-82 `refresh_url()` is the same unchecked `env_or("HARW_CODEX_OAUTH_REFRESH_URL", DEFAULT_REFRESH_URL)`. Lines 342-353 build `RefreshRequest{client_id, grant_type, refresh_token}` and POST to `refresh_url()`; line 356 `let body = response.text().await?;` again unbounded/untimed. This runs while holding the refresh lock acquired at line 331 (`acquire_refresh_lock`), confirming the "hangs while holding the lock" part of the finding.
- harw-cli/src/auth.rs:93 `let client = reqwest::Client::new();` — a bare client with no `.timeout(...)` call — is the client passed into `harw_oauth::exchange_code` for the login flow (lines 94-101).
- Cross-checked the production refresh path too: harw-provider-http/src/codex.rs:177-182 `refresh()` forwards whatever client it's given straight into `refresh_codex_tokens`, and the client built in harw-provider-http/src/lib.rs:1047-1052 (`http_client()`) only sets a redirect policy, no `.timeout()` either — so the missing-deadline problem is not confined to the CLI call site.
- Grepped the whole repo for `HARW_OAUTH_TOKEN_URL`, `HARW_CODEX_OAUTH_REFRESH_URL`, `HARW_OAUTH_AUTHORIZE_URL`: only flow.rs and codex_refresh.rs reference them, so there is no validation layer elsewhere (e.g. in harw-egress) that intercepts these env overrides — flow.rs/codex_refresh.rs import only secrecy/serde/serde_json/base64/std, never harw-egress's `EgressUrl` or similar. No test in flow.rs asserts scheme or timeout enforcement (grep for timeout/scheme/https/loopback in flow.rs only matches the doc-comment defaults).

Everything the finding cites reproduces byte-for-byte on the current working tree; I found no mitigating check anywhere else in the codebase. This is a genuine fail-open gap: an operator-controlled env var can silently redirect a PKCE code + verifier or a long-lived Codex refresh token to an arbitrary http/host, and a stalled/slow endpoint can hang the login and, worse, the refresh path while holding the cross-process refresh lock (codex_refresh.rs:331), since no timeout exists at any layer between the CLI/provider client construction and this code.

fixable_in_one_file=false because the fix genuinely spans two files as the finding states (harw-oauth/src/flow.rs and harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs need the URL-scheme guard and timeout/size-cap logic in both their respective functions), and a complete fix arguably also touches the client construction sites (harw-cli/src/auth.rs:93 and harw-provider-http/src/lib.rs:1047-1052) to actually set a request timeout, since neither `exchange_code` nor `refresh_codex_tokens` currently has any way to enforce a deadline other than relying on the caller's client.

ANSWER: Real. I could not refute it — no documented decision accepts this risk, and nothing elsewhere in the transport stack catches it before or after harw-oauth.

EVIDENCE

1. Env override has no scheme/host check, only blank-filtering.
`/home/user/Harwness/harw-oauth/src/flow.rs:36-41` (`env_or`) and the byte-identical copy at `/home/user/Harwness/harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs:69-74` do `std::env::var(var).ok().filter(|v| !v.trim().is_empty()).unwrap_or_else(...)`. No `url::Url::parse`, no scheme allowlist, anywhere in either file (checked with grep for `scheme|https` in harw-oauth/src — no hits outside doc comments). `HARW_OAUTH_TOKEN_URL` is consumed directly at `flow.rs:182` (`client.post(env_or("HARW_OAUTH_TOKEN_URL", DEFAULT_TOKEN_URL))`) and the PKCE `code_verifier`+authorization `code` go in the JSON body at `flow.rs:172-179`. `HARW_CODEX_OAUTH_REFRESH_URL` is consumed at `codex_refresh.rs:80-81`/`348-349`, carrying the long-lived Codex `refresh_token` (`codex_refresh.rs:342-352`).

2. Unbounded, timeout-less body read confirmed at both sites.
`flow.rs:188-189`: `let body = response.text().await?;` — no `Content-Length` check, no `bytes_stream` cap. `codex_refresh.rs:355-356`: identical pattern. Neither `exchange_code` nor `refresh_codex_tokens` wraps `.send()` or `.text()` in `tokio::time::timeout`; there is no size-limited read anywhere in either file.

3. Both real call sites use timeout-less clients — this is not "handled by the caller" as one might hope.
- CLI login: `/home/user/Harwness/harw-cli/src/auth.rs:93` — `let client = reqwest::Client::new();` then `runtime.block_on(harw_oauth::exchange_code(&client, ...))` (auth.rs:94-102). Plain `reqwest::Client::new()` has no default timeout.
- Codex refresh: `/home/user/Harwness/harw-provider-http/src/codex.rs:178` calls `harw_oauth::refresh_codex_tokens(client, ...)`. That `client` is built by `http_client()` at `/home/user/Harwness/harw-provider-http/src/lib.rs:1047-1052` — `reqwest::Client::builder().redirect(redirect_policy()).build()`, again no `.timeout()`. The crate does have a per-request timeout mechanism (`send_with_timeout` at `lib.rs:4332-4350`, which calls `builder.timeout(timeout).send()`), but that helper is only used for the main provider request path, not for the internal refresh call in `codex.rs:177-182`, which calls `client.post(refresh_url())...send()` directly with no `.timeout()`. So the one place a timeout convention exists in this codebase is deliberately not reused here — that's an omission, not a documented exception.
- The refresh also holds the cross-process refresh lock for the duration (`codex_refresh.rs:331`, `_lock` dropped only at function return), matching the finding's "hangs while holding the refresh lock" claim.

4. A proper answer already exists in the workspace and is simply not used here: `/home/user/Harwness/harw-egress/src/client.rs:110-127` (`build_client`) gives a `reqwest::Client` with a scoped DNS resolver, `no_proxy()`, `redirect::Policy::none()`, and a 10s `connect_timeout` (client.rs:42,124). `harw-oauth`'s `Cargo.toml` does not depend on `harw-egress` (grep found no match), and neither `flow.rs` nor `codex_refresh.rs` references it. So the mitigating machinery lives in the workspace but isn't wired to this code path — this is exactly the "M1 fail-open/skip-the-check" pattern the earlier hunt named, not an M2 split-across-layers case where another layer legitimately owns it.

5. No documented decision covers this. `grep -ri "HARW_OAUTH_TOKEN_URL\|HARW_CODEX_OAUTH_REFRESH_URL"` across the whole repo returns only the two source files — nothing in `docs/planning/70-decisions`, `docs/guides`, or the migration ledger. The module docs (`flow.rs:9-12`, `codex_refresh.rs:30-34`) explain *why* the endpoints are env-overridable (deploy without rebuild) but say nothing about scheme/host validation, timeouts, or body caps — silence on a risk is not a recorded acceptance of it. `harw-netsec` and `harw-security-hub` (also in my area) have no `reqwest`/`egress`/`scheme` references at all (grep, no files found), so there is no outer network guard in this codebase that would catch an arbitrary-scheme override or an unbounded/never-timing-out read before it reaches the socket.

I could not find any test asserting scheme rejection, a size cap, or a timeout for either `exchange_code` or `refresh_codex_tokens` — the existing unit tests (`flow.rs:210+`, `codex_refresh.rs` tests using `reqwest::Client::new()` at lines 505/525) only exercise URL construction and refresh bookkeeping, not the failure modes described.

VERDICT: real=true. The finding's every specific evidentiary claim checks out at the cited lines (and one more: `http_client()` in harw-provider-http, which I checked because the finding implies the refresh path in general lacks a timeout — it does, even one layer up). No CLAUDE.md/decisions/guides text documents accepting this; no other layer intercepts it; the one existing safe-client builder in the workspace (`harw-egress::build_client`) is not used by `harw-oauth`.

fixable_in_one_file=false, matching the finding's own `single_file: false`. A real fix needs at least: `harw-oauth/src/flow.rs` (URL validation + timeout/size cap around `exchange_code`), `harw-oauth/src/codex_refresh.rs` (same around `refresh_codex_tokens`), and ideally the two client-construction call sites — `harw-cli/src/auth.rs:93` and `harw-provider-http/src/lib.rs:1047-1052`/`codex.rs:178` — to actually pass a bounded client, since a fix inside `harw-oauth` alone can add its own `tokio::time::timeout` wrapper (defense in depth) without touching callers, but the "stalled endpoint hangs the login/refresh" half of the finding is only fully closed if the client itself also carries a timeout.

WHERE NEW CODE SHOULD LIVE (per `xtask/arch-policy.toml`): `harw-oauth` is layer `A` (application/composition, `may_depend_on = ["*"]`, `xtask/arch-policy.toml:322-323`); `harw-egress` is layer `I` (`xtask/arch-policy.toml:124-125`), and `I.may_depend_on` lower layers only while `A` may depend on anything — so `harw-oauth` is architecturally free to add a dependency on `harw-egress` and reuse `harw_egress::build_client`/`EgressPolicy` for the token/refresh HTTP calls instead of a bare `reqwest::Client`. The scheme/host validation (`url::Url`, https-only-with-loopback-exception) and the body-size cap belong as small helpers inside `harw-oauth` itself (next to `env_or` in both files, or factored into a shared `harw-oauth/src/http.rs` if the duplication between `flow.rs` and `codex_refresh.rs` is to be resolved at the same time), since `harw-oauth` is explicitly documented (module docs in both files) as the owner of these env-overridable endpoints.

title: Broken intra-doc link to harw_core::AgentSession::begin_approval: harw-protocol does not depend on harw-core
description: The default_timeout_at doc links [`harw_core::AgentSession::begin_approval`]. harw-protocol's only dependencies are harw-types, jiff, serde and serde_json, so rustdoc cannot resolve the path (broken_intra_doc_links). The workspace enforces no rustdoc lints, so nothing catches it. This is separate from the reported harw-egress lib.rs:13 link.
evidence: approvals.rs:165; harw-protocol/Cargo.toml [dependencies] = harw-types, jiff, serde, serde_json; the target exists at harw-core/src/session.rs:1840.
fix: Replace the link with plain code text (`harw_core::AgentSession::begin_approval`), as approvals.rs:193 already does for PendingApproval::is_timed_out.
test_idea: Central build: RUSTDOCFLAGS='-D rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links' cargo doc -p harw-protocol --no-deps.
reasons:
CONFIRMED — finding stands as reported.

Verified on the current working tree:

1. `/home/user/Harwness/harw-protocol/src/approvals.rs:165` reads exactly:
   `/// `requested_at + `[`harw_types::DEFAULT_APPROVAL_TIMEOUT`] — dieselbe`
   `/// Politik, die [`harw_core::AgentSession::begin_approval`] für Turn-lokale`
   This is rustdoc intra-doc-link syntax (`[`path`]`), not a plain code span.

2. `harw-protocol/Cargo.toml:11-18` `[dependencies]` = `harw-types`, `jiff` (workspace), `serde`, `serde_json` only. `grep -n "harw-core" harw-protocol/Cargo.toml` returns nothing — no path/crate dependency on `harw-core` exists anywhere in the manifest, dev-dependencies included (only `[dependencies]` section present at all). Rustdoc resolves intra-doc links against the crate's own dependency graph, so `harw_core::...` cannot resolve from within `harw-protocol`.

3. Target exists: `harw-core/src/session.rs` defines `pub fn begin_approval(...)` at line ~1839-1840 (confirmed by reading lines 1830-1850), so the link would be valid *if* `harw-protocol` depended on `harw-core` — it is purely a missing-dependency/unresolvable-path problem, not a typo in the method name.

4. No lint would catch this at build time: `Cargo.toml` `[workspace.lints.rust]` (root Cargo.toml:219-220) sets only `unsafe_code = "forbid"`; `harw-protocol/Cargo.toml:20-21` just inherits `[lints] workspace = true`. `harw-protocol/src/lib.rs:1-14` has only `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, no `#![warn(rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links)]` or `#![deny(rustdoc::all)]`. title: Findings export is opened before the is_file check: a FIFO at the path blocks forever, stalls posture requests and hangs shutdown
description: read_tail() calls File::open(path) and only afterwards checks metadata.is_file(). The module calls the export 'attacker-influenced input'. If a FIFO is placed at the path, open(O_RDONLY) blocks until a writer appears, so the NotAFile guard never runs. posture() calls this through spawn_blocking with no timeout (server.rs:600). Each request therefore hangs indefinitely and pins a blocking-pool thread. Because Tokio waits for blocking tasks at runtime drop, SIGTERM shutdown also hangs until systemd kills the process.

fix: Check fs::symlink_metadata(path) for is_file() before opening. Then open with O_NONBLOCK and O_NOFOLLOW (std::os::unix::fs::OpenOptionsExt::custom_flags with rustix/libc constants), and re-check is_file() on the opened handle. Also wrap the spawn_blocking await in tokio::time::timeout and report status 'unavailable' on timeout. The second part is in server.rs.

2. The module's own doc comment at `findings.rs:26` literally reads `# Limits (the file is attacker-influenced input)`, matching the finding's characterization of the threat model.
3. `harw-security-hub/src/config.rs:207-214` validates only that `findings.path` is absolute and that numeric limits are positive — no file-type check at load time, so nothing prevents the path from pointing at (or later being replaced by) a FIFO before a request triggers the read.

title: SecurityHub and harw-web Unix-socket servers have no connection cap, unlike netsec, node-transport and egress
description: harw-netsec (Semaphore, server.rs:540), harw-node-transport (slots, server.rs:161) and the egress proxy (proxy.rs:278) all bound concurrent connections. The SecurityHub accept loop and harw-web's serve_until spawn one task per accepted stream without limit. Any peer that can reach the socket (group harw-security, or the web socket's mode) can open connections until the process hits EMFILE, and then every other client is refused. In harw-web, SSE connections also never time out (server.rs:99-100). The same limit is enforced differently in each of the sibling daemons.

fix: Mirror netsec: add `max_connections` to the hub ServerConfig (default for example 256) and use an Arc<Semaphore> with try_acquire_owned before spawning. Move the permit into serve_connection and drop the stream when no permit is available. Do the same in harw-web BoundWebServer (a constant or WebServerConfig field).

Its ServerConfig (harw-security-hub/src/config.rs:101-118) has only max_contexts (a cap on stored security contexts, applied at server.rs:177 via ContextTable::with_capacity_limit) — unrelated to concurrent connections, and not consulted in the accept loop. harw-web's serve_until (harw-web/src/server.rs:420-514) likewise spawns one task per accepted stream at lines 494-511 with no permit; WebServerConfig (server.rs:229-232) has only socket_path, and grep for max_connections|Semaphore in harw-web/src returns zero matches. By contrast: harw-netsec/src/server.rs:524 builds Arc::new(Semaphore::new(service.settings.max_connections)) and line 540 gates spawn with try_acquire_owned before connections.spawn (line 552); harw-node-transport/src/server.rs:171 gates tokio::spawn (line 178) with Arc::clone(&self.inner.slots).try_acquire_owned(); harw-egress/src/proxy.rs:278 checks sessions.len() >= limits.max_connections and drops the stream instead of spawning. So the M2 claim (limit/accounting logic present in three sibling daemons but absent, inconsistently, in SecurityHub and harw-web) holds exactly as described, with all line numbers matching current content. title: uid_tenants and uid_principals accept aliased UID keys ('1000', '01000', '+1000', ' 1000'); the last one in string order silently wins
description: parse_uid trims the key and parses it as u32, which accepts leading zeros, a leading '+' and whitespace, so several distinct TOML keys map to the same uid. tenant_map and principal_map push every entry without a duplicate check. UidTenantMap::new and SecurityHubResolver::new collect them into a HashMap, so the entry that sorts last in the BTreeMap wins. A config such as `{"1000"="tenant-a", "01000"="tenant-b"}` is accepted, and the tenant uid 1000 is scoped to depends on key order. The SecurityHub policy rejects a duplicate uid rule for the same kind of mapping.
evidence: identity.rs:712-718 `key.trim().parse::<u32>()`; identity.rs:725-733 and 740-751 no duplicate check; identity.rs:325-329 HashMap collect; identity.rs:494 principals collected into HashMap; contrast harw-security-hub/src/policy.rs:188-192 'duplicate peer rule for uid'.
fix: In tenant_map and principal_map, keep a seen-uid set and return a new IdentityConfigError::DuplicateUid. Optionally accept only canonical decimal keys (no sign, no leading zeros, no whitespace).
test_idea: Parse `uid_tenants = { "1000" = "tenant-a", "01000" = "tenant-b" }` and assert build_resolver returns DuplicateUid; do the same for uid_principals. Central build: cargo test -p harw-web.
reasons: Confirmed on the current working tree (harw-web/src/identity.rs is clean, no uncommitted round-R15 changes to this file). parse_uid at identity.rs:712-718 is exactly `key.trim().parse::<u32>()`. Rust's integer FromStr accepts an optional leading '+' for unsigned types (only a leading '-' is rejected for unsigned, per the standard library's from_str_radix), and decimal parsing has no leading-zero restriction; trim() strips whitespace before parsing. So "1000", "01000", "+1000", and " 1000" all parse to uid 1000. tenant_map (identity.rs:725-734) and principal_map (identity.rs:740-751) iterate uid_tenants/uid_principals — both declared as BTreeMap<String,String> at identity.rs:648 and 652 — call parse_uid per key with no seen-uid/duplicate check, and push every (uid, value) pair into a Vec regardless of collisions. Those Vecs are then collected into a HashMap: UidTenantMap::new at identity.rs:322-329 (`entries: entries.into_iter().collect()`, field type HashMap<u32, TenantId> at line 319) and SecurityHubResolver::new at identity.rs:484-498 (`principals: principals.into_iter().collect()`, field type HashMap<u32, String> at line 471). Because BTreeMap iterates keys in ascending byte-lexicographic order and HashMap::collect lets a later pair overwrite an earlier one with the same key, the entry whose string key sorts last wins on collision — e.g. for {"1000"="tenant-a","01000"="tenant-b"}, "01000" < "1000" lexicographically ('0' 0x30 < '1' 0x31), so "1000" is visited last and tenant-a wins, matching the finding's claim. Confirmed by contrast that harw-security-hub/src/policy.rs:188-192 does enforce a duplicate check ('duplicate peer rule for uid') via a BTreeSet<u32> `seen.insert(rule.uid)` in Policy::validate, on a different (already-u32) peer-rule list — so the codebase has established precedent for rejecting duplicate uids elsewhere, but harw-web's string-keyed uid_tenants/uid_principals path has no equivalent check. Grepped the whole file for "seen"/"duplicate"/"Duplicate" — the only other hits (line 867-889) are an unrelated test helper tracking verify() calls, not a uid dedup guard. Grepped existing tests (lines ~1300-1450) covering tenant_map/principal_map: they cover invalid uid strings, blank tenant/principal, and mode gating, but there is no test with aliased/duplicate uid keys, so the gap is untested. This is a real, reproducible fail-open/aliasing bug (fits the hunt's M1/M2 pattern: silent last-wins instead of a rejected config), not a false positive. Fix is localized to a single file: harw-web/src/identity.rs — add a seen-uid set (e.g. HashSet<u32>) inside tenant_map (identity.rs:725-734) and principal_map (identity.rs:740-751), returning a new IdentityConfigError::DuplicateUid variant (added to the enum at identity.rs:657-681 and its Display impl at 683-708) when a uid repeats; optionally also restrict parse_uid (identity.rs:712-718) to canonical decimal keys (no sign, no leading zeros, no interior/leading/trailing whitespace beyond trim) to remove the aliasing at the source. No other crate/file needs a change; harw-web is arch-policy.toml layer "A" (xtask/arch-policy.toml:364-365), so the fix stays fully within this leaf-layer crate.

Confirmed, not refuted. harw-web/src/identity.rs:712-718 `parse_uid` does `key.trim().parse::<u32>()`. Rust's unsigned `FromStr` accepts an optional leading `+` and any number of leading zeros (well-documented std behavior: "+1000" and "01000" both parse to 1000); the explicit `.trim()` additionally folds in surrounding whitespace (" 1000"). So "1000", "01000", "+1000", " 1000" are four distinct TOML string keys in the `BTreeMap<String,String>` fields `uid_tenants`/`uid_principals` (identity.rs:648,652) that all collapse to uid 1000.

`tenant_map` (identity.rs:725-734) and `principal_map` (identity.rs:740-751) iterate the BTreeMap in lexicographic key order and push every `(uid, value)` pair into a `Vec` with no duplicate-uid check at all — confirmed by reading both functions end to end, no `seen`/`HashSet` logic present. The `Vec` is then collected into a `HashMap<u32, TenantId>` in `UidTenantMap::new` (identity.rs:322-329, `entries.into_iter().collect()`) and into `HashMap<u32, String>` in `SecurityHubResolver::new` (identity.rs:485-498, line 494 `principals.into_iter().collect()`). `HashMap::from_iter`/`collect` overwrites on duplicate keys in iteration order, so the entry whose string key sorts last (`" 1000" < "+1000" < "01000" < "1000"` in byte order) silently wins; nothing rejects the config.

Intent check: no decision doc, guide, or module comment documents this as acceptable. The module-level doc (identity.rs:1-64) and the config example (identity.rs:619-630) only ever show canonical decimal keys; nothing states aliasing is tolerated. `docs/planning/70-decisions/*` has no entry mentioning uid config or key canonicalization. Tests in this file (e.g. around identity.rs:1039-1450) cover invalid-uid, blank-tenant/blank-principal, and mode-mismatch errors but never a duplicate/aliased-uid case, so the gap is untested, not intentionally accepted.

"Handled elsewhere" check: the only place in-scope that does enforce a duplicate-uid invariant is `harw-security-hub/src/policy.rs:184-192`, but that guards a different config surface entirely — `SecurityPolicy.peers`, the Hub's own peer-rule list used for its `GET /v1/contexts` authorization — not `harw-web`'s `WebIdentityConfig`. I checked all callers of `WebIdentityConfig`/`IdentityConfigError` (`harw-web/src/server.rs`, `harw-web/src/lib.rs`, `harw-cli/src/web.rs`) and found no upstream canonicalization or duplicate-key rejection before `tenant_map()`/`principal_map()`/`build_resolver()` run. So the existence of `policy.rs`'s check is precedent for the invariant mattering, not evidence that this instance is already covered.

Blast radius is real but modest given severity "low": this is operator-authored TOML, not attacker input, but a copy-paste/leading-zero/whitespace slip silently reassigns a uid's tenant or expected principal based on string sort order rather than raising a startup error — exactly the kind of config-validation gap the R15 pattern list (M1/config validation) is hunting for.

Fix scope: adding an `IdentityConfigError::DuplicateUid` variant, a `Display` arm, and a `seen: HashSet<u32>` check in `tenant_map`/`principal_map` is confined to harw-web/src/identity.rs. I checked all external match sites on `IdentityConfigError` (only `harw-cli/src/web.rs:1404-1411`, a plain `assert_eq!` on one specific variant, not an exhaustive match) — adding a variant does not require touching that file. So `fixable_in_one_file: true` as the finding itself claims.

title: harw-web docs still say every decision comes from decide_route/PeerAuthorizer, but since H12 it is decide_resolved_route via LocalPeerIdentityResolver
description: The crate, router and meta docs describe the pre-H12 path. server::handle calls decide_resolved_route. handle_meta calls tier_permits directly on a resolver result. Identity comes from LocalPeerIdentityResolver, which also carries the tenant. The docs name decide_route and PeerAuthorizer as the only decision points, which is misleading exactly at the authority boundary.
evidence: lib.rs:37-41 `[server::handle] (privat) trifft keine eigene Zugriffsentscheidung — jede kommt aus [router::decide_route], das ausschließlich [authz::PeerAuthorizer] ... befragt.`; lib.rs:72-73 `[authz::tier_permits] und [router::decide_route] sind die einzigen Stellen`; router.rs:24-26 `[decide_route] fragt für die Berechtigungsstufe ausschließlich [crate::authz::PeerAuthorizer]`; meta.rs:26-27 `aufgelöst über denselben [crate::authz::PeerAuthorizer] wie jede Route`; actual: server.rs:685 `decide_resolved_route(&routes, resolved, &path, method)`, server.rs:787-791 resolver plus tier_permits.

reasons:
Finding confirmed on the current working tree (harw-web/src/{lib,router,meta,server,identity}.rs are clean per `git status --short`, so this is not a race with a concurrent edit).

Verified facts:
- lib.rs:37-41 states verbatim: "[server::handle] (privat) trifft keine eigene Zugriffsentscheidung — jede kommt aus [router::decide_route], das ausschließlich [authz::PeerAuthorizer] ... befragt." But server.rs:685 shows `let decision = decide_resolved_route(&routes, resolved, &path, method);` — `server::handle` calls `decide_resolved_route`, not `decide_route`. `decide_route` is not called anywhere in server.rs (grep confirms its only call sites are router.rs's own doctest/tests, router.rs:200/693 etc.).
- router.rs:250-257 shows `decide_resolved_route` takes `identity: Option<&ResolvedPeer>` and gets the tier via `identity.map(ResolvedPeer::tier)` (router.rs:256) — it takes no `&dyn PeerAuthorizer` argument at all, unlike `decide_route` (router.rs:210-218, which does `authorizer.tier_for(peer)`). So the claim that decisions come "ausschließlich" from a function that "ausschließlich PeerAuthorizer befragt" is false for the actual runtime path.
- lib.rs's own later section (51-59, the H12 addendum) contradicts the earlier passage: "Die Entscheidung bleibt bei [router::decide_resolved_route] ... der Mandant gelangt nur über [identity::ResolvedPeer::scope_op_context]" — i.e. the file documents both the stale claim and the corrected one, an internal inconsistency, not just an isolated stale line.
- lib.rs:72-73 repeats the stale "einzige Stellen" (only places) framing for `authz::tier_permits`/`router::decide_route`, again omitting `decide_resolved_route`.
- router.rs:24-29 ("Kein zweiter Autoritätspfad") describes only `decide_route`→`PeerAuthorizer` and never mentions `decide_resolved_route`, defined a few dozen lines below in the same file and the one actually wired into `server::handle`.

Actual code: server.rs:786-791 calls `resolve_identity(identity, peer, headers)` (the `LocalPeerIdentityResolver`) then `tier_permits(resolved.tier(), required)` directly — no `PeerAuthorizer` call in `handle_meta`. Scope: affects three files (harw-web/src/lib.rs:37-41,51-59,72-73; harw-web/src/router.rs:24-29; harw-web/src/meta.rs:26-28), matching the finding's own `single_file: false` — so not fixable in one file.

title: unwrap() in doctests of decide_route, from_registry and method_for
description: The binding rule forbids unwrap in doctests. Clippy does not check doctests.
evidence: L198 `let routes = WebRouteTable::from_registry(&registry).unwrap();`; L364 same; L435 `let routes = WebRouteTable::from_registry(&OperationRegistry::new()).unwrap();`
fix: Use `?` and end each doctest with `# Ok::<(), harw_web::error::WebError>(())`.
test_idea: Central build: cargo test -p harw-web --doc.
reasons: Confirmed on the current tree: harw-web/src/router.rs contains exactly three unwrap() calls, all inside executable (non-ignored) ```rust doctest fences: L198 (fence 190-208), L364 (fence 359-366), L435 (fence 431-437), per `grep -n` for both the fences and the unwrap() calls. These are genuine doctests (cargo test --doc compiles and runs them), so the binding rule 'no unwrap/expect/panic! in library code OR tests/doctests' applies and is violated; clippy indeed does not lint inside doctests, so this class of violation is real and easily missed. from_registry returns Result<Self, WebError> (router.rs:367) and WebError is public (error.rs:51, re-exported via lib.rs:152), so the proposed `?` + `# Ok::<(), harw_web::error::WebError>(())` fix is valid and confined to this one file/these three doctest blocks.

Confirmed at harw-web/src/router.rs:198, :364, :435 — three doctest bodies call `.unwrap()` on `WebRouteTable::from_registry(...)` (returns `Result<Self, WebError>`), inside the examples for `decide_route` (L198), `WebRouteTable::from_registry` itself (L364), and `method_for` (L435). Rustdoc compiles/runs doctests as separate mini-crates; clippy never runs on them, so `cargo clippy -D warnings` cannot catch this — the finding's premise holds.

I looked for a carve-out and found none: xtask's gates (gate_arch.rs, gate_privileges.rs, gate_edges.rs, gate_warden.rs, gates.rs) have no doc-comment/doctest scanner — grep for "doctest"/"scan_doc" across xtask/src returns nothing relevant. docs/planning/70-decisions/ contains only DEC-001..008 (passed=true, judge-cheap-reads, provider-limits, no-parallel-builds, small-scopes-waves, model-agnostic, worker-rights, no-tui) and none mention unwrap or doctests. .github/copilot-instructions.md:13 states the rule with no doctest exception: "No unwrap(), expect() or panic! in library code or tests." The computed task brief is explicit that the binding rule covers tests/doctests too. So this is neither documented as intentional nor enforced/handled elsewhere.

It is also not an isolated slip that could be argued as "the author's deliberate style": the same crate already follows the correct convention elsewhere — harw-web/src/security.rs:117 uses `# Ok::<(), harw_web::security::SecurityError>(())`, harw-web/src/peer.rs:106 uses `# Ok(())`, and other in-scope crates (harw-egress/src/client.rs:107, harw-egress/src/relay.rs:51, harw-egress/src/lib.rs:53, harw-egress/src/proxy.rs:61, harw-security-hub/src/policy.rs:94) all use `?`-based doctests ending in `# Ok(...)`. router.rs is a real outlier against the crate's own established pattern, not a design decision.
